Latest Update: I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance.
  • In a recent development, developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal.
  • Recent findings suggest that the first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance. Voyaging uncharted waters may appear foolish to some, yet folly and heroism can often appear the same to the undiscerning eye," so says the voice of Johannes Zuch - creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' behind Leonida's latest favourite indie darling art game, Tenebrae Lux. It's pretentious, it's deeply up its own arse, and it's awkward and off-putting to play. A must-review for Eurogamer.

In a recent development, developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal. Jason is quick to dismiss Tenebrae Lux in company, but once Cal slinks off home - hungover and dreary - I slide the disc back into my JoyStation console and sink my teeth back into it. Jason loves this stuff, really. He only keeps Time Jackers: Rewind installed so his mates don't judge him.

Recent findings suggest that the first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name. It's Latin for 'darkness and light', or something similar. Is this riffing on Clair Obscur, which is French for 'light dark'? No, it's too cerebral for that - too plodding and navel-gazey. Sandfall Interactive wouldn't be this pretentious. Maybe it's a pastiche of Dear Esther, then, drawing on the tenets and schema of the 'walking simulator' genre and using that washed-out film noir aesthetic. But then, it's too wordy for that, with too many interactive and puzzle-adjacent elements. Ah, it must be mocking The Witness, instead - there's the telltale lighthouse, the 'I'm definitely not telling you where to go and what to do' internal narration, and of course the fingerprints of Johannes Zuch are all over it. Johannes Zuch, Jonathan Blow - see how they braided them together? (Sorry).

In a recent development, whilst this has been created by Rockstar as a pastiche - as much loving send-up as it is withering take down - and designed to make a quick joke in the early 'Feng Shui' mission, the game is playable from start to finish if you so desire. You boot it up by inserting a physical disc, too, which is funny given the context. And it's good! Well, not good good, but it's a proper brainteaser, and ribs 2016's The Witness with such knowledge and (I think?) respect that it's hard not to be charmed by Rockstar's game-within-a-game. There are collectibles to be found that riff on Mark Z. Danielewski's House of Leaves, too, a knowing nod to the most try-hard of all try-hard literature.

Within seconds of the title screen, too, you're presented with a game-within-a-game-within-a-game. You must clear four boards filled with puzzle pieces as the protagonist mutters something mysterious and weird in his posh voice. Do so, and you unlock the door to the next location. Head up to a bunker, and you'll see a room filled with various clues - maybe it's a flashing lamp flickering in morse code, maybe it's a malfunctioning clock presenting a maths puzzle, maybe it's a pricetag on a record that changes on every visit, maybe it's a photograph with anomalous elements, maybe it's a "Developed Using Zuchworks Engine" easter egg hidden in the environment. You need to keep your wits about you, because one of these clues changes every time you enter - and the clue corresponds to a date that changes on a calendar on the wall.

In a recent development, you can look up a guide if you need to, or you can spend far too long figuring out how all this relates to the telephone you can find in the room on your own, like muggins here, before opening up the path to the next puzzle. Look at the image below to see the level of record-keeping and brainteasing this bizarre little game prompted from me. I will say, the sense of achievement you get from playing around with this stuff is pretty remarkable, given - let's not forget I'm actually playing Grand Theft Auto 6 whilst I'm wandering around in the black and white murk trying to complete a puzzle game for no actual reward.

Industry observers note that the bunker room is, by far, the hardest part of Tenebrae Lux. From here, things ease up: you need to figure out the right sequence of glyphs on a bridge, and then put some distance between yourself and a curious and rather creepy suited man that's seemingly figuring things out ahead of you in a location inspired by, I think, The Backrooms (or Portal, or Superliminal, or maybe something else entirely. Who knows what Zuch was thinking?).

"With the last enigma finally mastered," the narrator drones in his bumbling monotone, "I step forward into the void, the shadows swallow, consuming all, and then finally the sweet embrace of darkness of which there is no end." 'You have just experienced a Johannes Zuch experience', Tenebrae Lux tells me, before cutting to the best joke of the whole thing: the credits roll much akin to something Hideo Kojima would produce.

So, what do you get out of all of this? Well - just like real puzzle games in the real world - nothing, really. If you've not completed one of the other three fully playable games in GTA 6, you will get a trophy/achievement. But given the main game is all about Jason and Lucia's desperate scramble to escape the poverty trap, to try and break free of the cycle of debt, violence, and consequence that keeps them clinging to Leonida's seedy underbelly, there's no monetary reward. There's no 'progress' in the sense of the protagonist's shared story.

Even in terms of your own cold, hard, mathematical 'completion' you only need to boot each of the four games up once in order to work towards GTA 6's 100% completion. So what's the point of all this? Why did I spend the better part of 90 minutes trying to figure out how to find a sliver of light in the dark in Tenebrae Lux? The game is a wonderful pastiche in that, essentially, it's not really saying anything. You can probably project some vague meaning onto it if you wish - I'm pretty certain the protagonist literally 'finds himself' at the end - but glib little readings like that are ten-a-penny in this genre.

I think the most impressive thing about Tenebrae Lux is that it exists. You're teased with it in an early mission - Rockstar may as well say 'look, we put a game in a game, lol' - but it's more than that. This is what happens when Rockstar's 4700-plus developers are given the room to… develop. Tenebrae Lux could very easily have been a non-interactive experience, a quick, cheap joke shown over-the-shoulder taking a drive-by pop shot at Johnathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck, or any and all of the above. Or maybe it could be a 'vertical slice', an incomplete demo, a teaser. But it's not, because nothing about GTA 6 is quick or cheap.

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6, in every single conceivable way, is a premium experience - part-sandbox, part-simulation, part-otherworld. To create not just one, but four fully playable and completable games within that framework is showboating, sure, but to make that game actually good and - perhaps controversially - even better than some of the games it's pastiching… Well, it's just rubbing salt in the wound, really.

A code for the game was provided by Cal Hampton.

In a recent development, building a modern web API is only half the battle. Ensuring it is secure, resilient, and capable of handling malicious traffic is what separates a hobby project from a production-ready service. When building highly scalable applications, we typically lean on stateless architectures. However, features like token revocation and rate limiting require state.

Sources indicate that in this guide, we will explore the architectural concepts behind building a secure API using FastAPI, Redis, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SlowAPI. We will break down the theory, the tech stack, and the flow of data—without getting bogged down in the code.

Before diving into the architecture, it is crucial to understand the role each tool plays in our security model:.

It has been revealed that security starts with how you manage your secrets. The first step in our architectural journey is setting up a configuration file and a local environment file.

Hardcoding secret keys, database URLs, or algorithm types directly into your application is a severe security risk. Instead, we load these from environment variables. The application uses a settings manager to read variables like the Redis host, port, the JWT secret key, the algorithm (typically HS256), and the token expiration time. This ensures that sensitive data stays out of your version control system.

To handle rate limiting and token tracking, we need a connection to Redis. Because FastAPI is inherently asynchronous, we initialize an asynchronous Redis client.

According to recent reports, redis acts as the central state-holder for our API. By using Redis, we ensure that even if our API is running on five different servers behind a load balancer, the rate limits and the token blacklists remain globally synchronized.

According to recent reports, next, we establish the utility functions that handle the cryptographic heavy lifting. This step is divided into two main parts:.

Here, we initialize the FastAPI application and attach slowapi.

slowapi needs a way to identify the client making the request. By default, it uses the client's IP address. We attach the limiter to the application state and register an exception handler. This ensures that if a user breaches the rate limit, the API gracefully returns a "429 Too Many Requests" error instead of crashing.

According to recent reports, we also set up a dependency that acts as a security guard for our protected routes. This dependency intercepts incoming requests, extracts the token, and decodes it. It then checks Redis to see if the token has been blacklisted (for example, if the user logged out before the token expired). If the token is valid and not blacklisted, the request proceeds; otherwise, a "401 Unauthorized" error is thrown.

Recent findings suggest that the login endpoint is where the magic happens. When a user submits their credentials, the API verifies the username and password. In a production scenario, this involves querying a database; in our example, we verify it against a hardcoded credential.

Once the credentials are validated, the API generates a JWT. To ensure we can invalidate this token later if needed, we store the token in Redis with a time-to-live (TTL) that matches the token's expiration time. Finally, the token is returned to the client, which will store it and send it in the Authorization header of future requests.

Finally, we create a route that requires both authentication and rate limiting.

Before the route's logic even executes, two things happen:.

If the client passes both security checks, they are granted access to the highly secure data provided by the route.

Sources indicate that to validate this system, you would conceptually walk through several test scenarios. First, you test the login flow with correct and incorrect credentials to ensure tokens are only issued to valid people.

Industry observers note that next, you test the rate limit by rapidly firing requests at the protected route to ensure the "429 Too Many Requests" response triggers. Finally, you test the security guard by trying to access the route with no token, an expired token, and a manually blacklisted token to ensure the API correctly denies access in all scenarios.

Building a secure API requires layering defenses. By combining FastAPI's speed, Redis's fast state management, JWT's stateless authentication, and slowapi's rate-limiting capabilities, you create a system that is both robust and scalable.

While this foundational text explains the core concepts, moving to production requires adding token refresh flows, implementing per-user rate limiting (rather than just IP-based), deploying Redis with high availability, and ensuring your secrets are managed by a secure vault. These practices will ensure your API remains secure as your user base grows.

AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the company into a leadership crisis.
  • On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the tech giant into a leadership crisis.
  • Investors may be relieved to have Huang back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the company into a leadership crisis. Investors may be relieved to have Huang back. But the events of the past two weeks have shown just how much Nvidia—and the wider AI industry—still depends on one man. The board said it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before reinstating Huang and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Its investigation remains open, however, and Nvidia has declared additional measures to address national security and compliance concerns. Huang’s departure also raised questions about Nvidia’s maturity as a corporate institution. In an analysis published shortly after Huang’s resignation, Andy Thurai, founder and principal analyst at The Field CTO, pointed to companies like Apple and IBM that spend years preparing their next generation of leaders. “That separates a mature corporate entity from a founder-led juggernaut,” he wrote. Huang is back, but Nvidia still needs to prepare for a future without him. Meanwhile, another major artificial intelligence company was making history on Wall Street. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, went public on November 19, pricing its shares at $83 in one of the largest initial public offerings in history. At that price, every one of an estimated 96% of the company’s employees held equity worth more than $1 million, according to data from Hill.com reported by CNN. The stock opened at $111.50 before closing its first trading day at $97.17. Investors who bought at the IPO price made money, but those who bought when trading opened were already sitting on losses. Both developments come at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. Billions of dollars continue to pour into the sector, but how much money are the companies receiving those investments actually making? And how long will investors be willing to wait? Judah Taub, managing partner at Hetz Ventures, thinks investors need to separate their excitement about AI from their assessment of the businesses behind it. “AI isn’t a bubble. But the way we’re financing AI might be,” he tells Fast Company. “The internet wasn’t a bubble, but many internet companies were. AI will be exactly the same.” AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology. THE MONEY BEHIND THE AI BOOM Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The company closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker. Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise? Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players. “Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub notes. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.” Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products. “The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.” That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the company is betting on. In a recent analysis for Fast Company, Mark Sullivan highlighted how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve owners as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices. Complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing. “The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe says. She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning. “I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she says. For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations. Now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance. THE BILL IS COMING DUE Investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology. Kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management company Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more quickly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save. “The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley says. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.” Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive. Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost. Some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified. The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can quickly become expensive. Airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with. “Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Company. This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each new generation of frontier models? Companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow. “I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.” WHO GETS THE VALUE? Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software. Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods. “There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.” His company combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient. “Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen says. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?” Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work. “These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says. Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify. For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most vital operations. “The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary. A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running. And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want. During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.” He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them. WHAT A CORRECTION COULD CHANGE A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money. O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models. “For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.” But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves. Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies. Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward. AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses. “We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns. Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed. For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them. Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work.

“These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he states.

Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify.

For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most important operations.

It has been revealed that “The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he indicates in written commentary.

A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running.

And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want.

During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.”.

In a recent development, he argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them.

A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money.

O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models.

Sources indicate that “For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.”.

But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a organization can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves.

Industry observers note that ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies.

Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward.

AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses.

“We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns.

It has been revealed that huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed.

Industry observers note that for much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers confirmed, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them.

Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are?
  • Recent findings suggest that right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea.
  • Called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are? Well, I've got some news for you. Keep on reading below if you'd like some very minor spoilers for the early game of GTA 6, spoilers for GTA 5, as well as some information about how the upcoming game links to GTA 5 and other Rockstar games.

Recent findings suggest that right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea. In the first hour or so of GTA 6, when you finally get control of Jason and head to your first property (the green stilted house) in the Leonida Keys, you will be able to explore a little. On my way to do a workout - you need to keep Jason a peak physical instrument for his work's sake, right? Right? - I happened upon a fitness magazine resting on a table on the decking out front.

Called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles. There's Morning Glory, where Nolan Crockett jacks you with his early workout; Skindecent Exposure, a photo spread about why beaches are 'crazy' places to work out; Shrediquette, a piece dedicated to proper in-gym decorum; and Twilight Tantra, an interview feature and yoga masterclass with 'gerontophile' Fabien LaRouche.

Recent findings suggest that hang on, Fabien LaRouche… isn't that the French wellness guru and shyster that was a "close friend" to Amanda De Santa in Grand Theft Auto 5? Yes, yes it is. In fact, Fabien played quite a large role in that game, acting as the antagonistic force that eventually fractured Michael and Amanda's relationship. After conducting an affair under the guise of 'yoga lessons', Amanda left our protagonist, and moved in with Fabien, taking Michael's kids - Jimmy and Tracy - with her. In a totally healthy and normal way, you could follow their new life via updates posted to GTA's Facebook surrogate, LifeInvader. It's clear the kids never liked the pretentious, annoying man - but for Amanda, the penny is a little slower to drop. Eventually, Amanda and Michael reconcile their differences - with the latter whalloping Fabien in the process. The married couple pledge to resolve their differences, and Fabien is never seen again.

Until GTA 6, at least. Here, in what we assume is supposed to be 2025 or 2026, it's been about 13 years since we last saw the character (it is widely agreed that GTA 5 is set in 2013 - the game's original launch year). And it seems that the events surrounding Michael and his family really did a number on Fabien. Which - of course - he blamed on the universe, rather than taking any personal responsibility. Naturally.

"Ever since the karmic decay of Los Santos was made perfectly clear to him in the early 2010s, yoga instructor Fabien LaRouche has been on an epic pilgrimage of enlightenment through the remotest ashrams and finest 5-star resorts and plastic surgery retreats of The East," reads the Body Copy article. "Having completed his chakric education and returned to the United States, we meet with him on the final week of his six-month residency at Dwindle Wood Retirement Community.".

Here, the article goes on to explore Fabien's penchant for older women - he seems to like their nature, their desire to learn about self-improvement and wellness, and (perhaps most importantly) their bank accounts. "Being over the hill doesn't necessarily mean you have nothing left to live for," he opines in the article. Thanks for that, Fabien.

It's interesting to see - very early in the game and quite plainly telegraphed - that Rockstar is willing to reintroduce us to people from previous games. This isn't a megaton addition by any means - Fabien was never a 'main character' - but I love that a nod to him, in a feature tucked away at the back of a magazine, sets the scene for more cameos, perhaps, later in the game. It shows us, nice and early, that GTA 5 and GTA 6 are indeed connected. By inference, then, we know that GTA 4 is included in that same picture; there were recurring characters in GTA 5 that appeared in GTA 4, after all - Patrick McReary, Johnny Klebitz, Rocco Pelosi and more come to mind.

It may seem like a small thing, but it's just another example of Rockstar using its expansive toolset, ridiculous budget, and well-established legacy to inject a sense of scale into the world of Grand Theft Auto 6. There are other nods to the universe out there, too. I won't spoil them here, but I've been a little bit dewy-eyed to hear rumours of some of the other nods to Rockstar titles hidden in the world of Leonida: it makes all the experiences I've had in past games, the emotional response I've had to previous Rockstar worlds, feel in some way valid and meaningful here, too. I'm looking forward to seeing what other little secrets await me across the keys and into the glowing neon promise of Vice City proper.

Industry observers note that did anything notable happen this week? Not that I can remember. The weather was quite rainy - will that do? I'm just being silly, of course. We've had - and I suppose are still having - an historic week in video games, as Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives. It's dominated everything and I fear it's going to dominate this article too. But a reminder: next week is our "Not-GTA Week", so we'll be making a concerted effort to talk about games, probably smaller games, that aren't Godzilla blockbusters.

As you know, this is our regular feature where we say a bit about the games we've been playing this week. This week, rather a lot of us have been playing GTA 6, as you can imagine, and discovering various things about it. But not all of us. Connor, ever the contrarian, has been continuing his race to level 60 in World of Warcraft: Forever, and he's agonisingly close to getting there.

In a recent development, but enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago.

According to recent reports, it probably comes as no surprise that I'm - much like the rest of the world - playing GTA 6 right now. While I found Chapter 1 to be quite a slow start, and where I felt somewhat restricted, I've now started Chapter 2 and found myself enjoying stealing cars, jamming along to the radio, and simply exploring Leonida - and all the strange happenings that come with it. There's so much to see and do!

Sources indicate that I'm looking forward to deviating from the main missions for a while to do a spot of bird-watching (I like birds a lot, alright) and seeing what other side activities Leonida has to offer outside of the criminal lifestyle at the core of things. I'm also trying to be the best partner possible to both Jason and Lucia, but I'm itching to cause a bit of trouble soon... Hurting NPCs comes with so much guilt this time around though!

It has been revealed that it's slow, it's awkward, it's weird, and it's hard. It's a perfect Eurogamer game, right? Right? GTA 6's in-game lampoon of Jonathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck and - weirdly - Mark Z. Danielewski is a wonderful bit of top-shelf pastiche. It goes to show just how much fun Rockstar had making GTA 6, and the freedom its dev team had to install as much depth and satire in just about every nook and cranny conceivable. Don't sleep on Tenebrae Lux, it's genuinely satisfying to complete.

In a recent development, I'm not, historically, the biggest GTA fan - although I've absolutely got a soft spot for Vice City's sublime mood - so I wasn't quite as excited to play GTA 6 as some. But it took, oh I dunno, about 30 seconds before I was sold. This thing has style. And everything else a billion dollars and some incredible development talent gets you. And it's those because-we-can details that have, in my first few hours, left the biggest impression. I spent a good five minutes just marveling at Jason dance - specifically the way his little stationary wiggle (perfectly timed to the radio beat!) shifts seamlessly into a wiggle-strut when you hit the forward button.

Industry observers note that I love the way the setting sun seems to shine just right through the clouds when the moment calls, and those perfect needle drops. And careening through the night - amid the driving rain and smear of taillights, Kylie classic Spinning Around booming on the radio and Jason rocking a recently acquired, slightly improbable hat - this extravagant, ridiculous thing had me completely transfixed. I'm genuinely, unexpectedly excited to see where it takes me next.

Assuming there's lots of Grand Theft Auto 6 in this article, I'll save you from my own early impressions of this week's blockbuster release. Instead, you get more tales from an MMO. It is what it is!

I'm level 58 right now, pushing my way into the endgame dungeons. I've almost maxed all my professions, and am gradually getting gear that should serve me well when the raids are added next month.

In a recent development, but forget all that. I got a salt shaker! As a leatherworker, you can buy a salt shaker from engineers for a little bit of gold on the auction house. These are more important than you'd assume. With them you can make one refined deeprock salt every three days - a high-end crafting material. Rather than hoard these for fancy gear, I just sold 'em back to the auction house. They're current going for 50 gold a pop on my server, which is fantastic passive income.

In a recent development, this is important because I'm presently saving for an epic mount: a process that hit a major roadbump after I unlocked my secondary class specialisation for 50 gold, and then blew way more than that on unlocking all the available skills (that I likely won't use) from my druid trainer (for no good reason). I'm currently sitting on 232 gold as of writing. There's a long way to go to 1000, but hey, that's the game.

According to recent reports, I can't imagine anyone changing the radio station when Drive by The Cars begins during that first moment of proper uninterrupted freedom. The buttons to do that might as well not even be there. If you did, we're completely different people.

I'm not very far in but my major impressions of GTA 6 so far are: the performances and their presentation are wonderful, the game controls a bit sludgily and feels like it's not quite in focus on PS5, and I really like DIY.

In a recent development, let's take that middle one, that criticism: I'm sure this will lift as I get used to the game and how it moves, and how the characters work. It's also just a fact of life, so to speak, that it's going to struggle a bit on PS5 rather than PS5 Pro. And I'm nitpicking; on the whole, this thing is staggeringly technically impressive.

In a recent development, the latter point, DIY: it's absurd how much detail Rockstar has put into you doing up your shack. I especially like how it's not boring. A deeper thought related to this, and to the rest of the game, is the fantasy of self-improvement GTA 6 delivers. In GTA 6, as in all GTA games I think, you can drastically alter your life's fortunes in mere moments. I set about doing up my shack in a way I could never do in real life given a week or a month, but here, I did it in moments. That appeals to me greatly.

In a recent development, honourable mention to Star Wars: Galactic Racer which I finally played this week. Love the speed, love Biddy Blas, and also really gel with the Roguelike approach, whereby you take the game in 'runs' to see how far you can progress each time. Cracking game.

Apple has removed an AI chatbot from the App Store after it sent inappropriate messages to children.

Recent findings suggest that artificial Intelligence has become a part of everyday life for a lot of people, and it has even been used by children in different way. There are schools that are solely focused on AI learning, while AI-powered toys became all the rage last Christmas.

More recently, an app on the Apple iOS store came under fire for reportedly sending inappropriate messages to younger consumers. Talkie, developed by Shanghai-based MiniMax, allows you to pick different AI characters to talk to.

While the app does have an 18+ rating on stores, it is still accessible to children, with users noting that many of these messages come with adult tones and language.

Following investigations by ABC News in Australia and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, the app has been removed from the App Store.

This also came after campaigners urged the developers to put better verification methods in place, so they could really see who was using the app and remove the ability to access certain content.

As per the report, the Talkie app was removed back in 2024 on the grounds of including “objectionable user-generated content,” but returned as a download after MiniMax released a newly introduced version in 2026.

Additionally, the app developers noted that most user access ‘stimulating’ content on there to help with everyday tasks and learning, but others have dipped into the companionship side of things.

According to recent reports, back in October of last year, data revealed that 42% of high schoolers knew someone or, have themselves used AI for companionship. One in five of those teenagers admitted to being in a romantic relationship with AI, too.

Apple introduces newly introduced 18+ age restrictions for dating apps and romantic AI companions.

China bans AI “boyfriends” and “girlfriends” over addiction and birth rate concerns.

Gen Alpha boys are preferring “AI girlfriends” over real ones.

In a different report, 40% of adults noted that they would date an AI chatbot, saying they may have already flirted with one too.

Some AI entities have had to remove their ‘adult modes’ due to investor pressure.

Can potential clients find you using AI?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing.
  • Industry observers note that A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing.
  • If you’re running a solo business, you’ve probably thought about how people find you online.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing. At the end of the interview, I asked her how she found me. She replied, “ChatGPT.”  If you’re running a solo business, you’ve probably thought about how people find you online. Maybe you even track the information by asking or through a “How did you find me?” question on your website. Many people now ask an AI chatbot for a recommendation, the same way they’ve typed questions into Google for years. No matter how you feel about using AI tools personally, AI search is something that may have more and more of an impact on your business over time. AI as the fresh recommendation engine For a long time, getting found online meant search engine optimization (SEO), or showing up in Google results by publishing content like a blog. The newer version is AEO (answer engine optimization) or GEO (generative engine optimization). The idea is that AI tools might “find” you the way Google once did. AEO and SEO share the same fundamentals. AI tools pull from publicly available information on the Internet, so the more you put out there, the easier you are to find. In BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey, 45% of consumers said they used ChatGPT or another AI tool to get recommendations for local businesses. A year earlier, it was 6%. That’s a big jump in a single year. The survey looked at local businesses, so it may not line up exactly with the work you do, but directionally it suggests that more and more people are turning to AI search to find what they’re looking for. Make sure you have a consistent online presence Like Google, AI tools look for an authoritative answer to whatever question someone asks. SEO has long focused on ranking in Google by following a set of “rules.” To me, AEO feels more like a wide-open, unclaimed field. No one quite understands it yet, though many people are trying to influence the AI search results. You can’t control the algorithms or LLMs, but you can control some of the narrative when Google Search or AI search finds you. AI tools piece together a description of you from all of these sources. Your website Your website is an obvious source for who you are and what you do. Your About and Products/ Services pages are good places to start. Make sure they’re up to date with the information you’d want someone to know or find. From there, you might add content that answers the questions potential clients are likely to ask. My website includes an FAQs section to help the algorithms and LLMs understand me better. Content also increases the likelihood that you’ll appear in search results, AI or otherwise. A blog works, and so does a publicly available newsletter. Case studies and testimonials help too, especially when they include client names and outcomes (with permission, of course). Your content on other sites Content on other sites gives AI tools something to cite when it answers someone’s question. It might be a podcast episode where you were a guest, or an article you wrote for someone else’s website. YouTube videos and social media posts count as well. Claim your business profile Google Business Profile is the original way to claim your business and correct its information. It’s worth setting up if you serve a local area, but for many online service providers (like me) it wasn’t necessary. In November 2026, OpenAI rolled out a beta of Businesses in ChatGPT, which lets a business claim and manage its listing. It’s in beta and open to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S. Once your business is verified, you can update its details. You’ll even be able to see how often ChatGPT mentions your business in its answers and how many people click through to your website. A LinkedIn Company Page works for a one-person business, too. I have one, and it highlights up when people search on LinkedIn. AI is one more way people ask for information I’ll admit: I immediately claimed my business profile in ChatGPT when I heard it was available. It only took a few minutes to verify my website and identity, and then I could see what ChatGPT “knows” about me. I also blueprint to track how many times ChatGPT mentions me (currently sitting at 19). Word of mouth still keeps my pipeline full, because people know the type of work I do. But I can’t ignore that people are also turning to AI chatbots for recommendations.

In a recent development, word of mouth still keeps my pipeline full, because people know the type of work I do. But I can’t ignore that people are also turning to AI chatbots for recommendations.

#230536. What if Vampire Survivors met Grand Theft Auto 2? Maniac is a brilliant mash-up that dares to ask that question

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (933 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

What if Vampire Survivors met Grand Theft Auto 2? Maniac is a brilliant mash-up that dares to ask that question

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that what would you get if you combined the chaotic top-down action of old-school Grand Theft Auto 2 with the chaotic top-down action of Vampire Survivors?
  • Your goal is simple: survive for as long as you can or until the 20-minute clock hits zero.
  • Sources indicate that maniac's debt to GTA is clear, and its chaotic action is brilliantly realised as it channels the compelling rhythms of a Survivors-style roguelite, where randomness in items and level layout makes each run fresh as you strive to unlock new characters, progressing a little further each time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what would you get if you combined the chaotic top-down action of old-school Grand Theft Auto 2 with the chaotic top-down action of Vampire Survivors? That's the question Soldat and King Arthur's Gold developer Transhuman asked when it started working on 2024's roguelite shooter Maniac. The result is a delight, yet Maniac remains frustratingly underappreciated.

Your goal is simple: survive for as long as you can or until the 20-minute clock hits zero. Throughout that time, your secondary objective is to create as much mayhem as possible - painting the road with the blood of your foes, slamming cars into buildings, performing drive-bys as you rampage across the procedurally-generated city. The more carnage you cause, the higher your Wanted level, until you're fending off police and the military.

Sources indicate that maniac's debt to GTA is clear, and its chaotic action is brilliantly realised as it channels the compelling rhythms of a Survivors-style roguelite, where randomness in items and level layout makes each run fresh as you strive to unlock new characters, progressing a little further each time. It's a relatively slight experience, as its £4 price tag reflects, featuring a single compact map, just six characters, and barely any permanent progression. But Maniac makes a spirited argument for a return to a simpler time when GTA was all about shooting cops, stealing cars, and indiscriminately murdering pedestrians rather than the 'everything' game it is today.

Maniac is also a game that feels like it's trying to make good on an idea many of us had when we first played GTA 1 & 2 all those years ago: what would a better-looking, more advanced version of that look like? And for developer Michał Marcinkowski, Maniac's genesis also harkens back to an earlier time. "When I was 12, I used to come back from school and play the demo of GTA 1," he tells me over email. "It was top-down and time-limited, and all I'd do was try to cause as much chaos as possible within the 20 minutes of the demo.".

Recent findings suggest that and there's perhaps a hint of a 12-year-old's exuberance to Maniac. There's the bright colour palette and gleeful chaos of its physics-driven mechanics, the adrenaline rush its aggressive enemy AI creates, and its absurd roster of playable characters, which range from Little Girl to Hotdog Guy. "Each [character] is a bit of me and a bit of you," Marcinkowski explains. "We all have a drunk Santa in us. We all have a pathetic hot-dog-suit guy inside of us. Each character failed at something and is lashing out.".

As each new Grand Theft Auto game pushes further into realism, the idea of recreating the rampages seen in classic GTA feels increasingly unpalatable, but Maniac's colourful cartoon aesthetic means it can get away with more. One Achievement, with a flourish of old-school bad-taste humour, challenges players to destroy five school buses using an airstrike ability called Santa's Little Helpers. And that level of irreverent, chaotic lunacy escalates the deeper into each session you get, particularly as your Wanted level climbs: if you antagonise law enforcement enough here, they eventually break out a game-ending nuke.

"This comes back to being 12," Marcinkowski claims. "Nukes are just cool. I wanted the game to end with a bang, and what's more maniacal and exaggerated than a nuke? So that idea was with me for more than 20 years.".

Core to Maniac's design is the ability to change from a Survivors-like auto-shooter to a standard shooter where you're able to control your aim. The latter option is, I think, the more fitting one, particularly given how much driving you do. If you squint, it almost feels like a GTA 2 clone. And while the Vampire Survivors inspirations are plentiful - including its now-standard three-option upgrade system - the GTA elements are clearly the more prevalent.

It might not play exactly like a GTA game, but it certainly captures the series' early days spirit. And Marcinkowski says he's surprised more developers haven't tried to riff on GTA: "You'd expect the most popular game in the world to have hundreds of clones, but that's not the case." There may be a reason for that.

As big as modern-day GTA is, clones are apparently much less popular. "When you look at the sales data, particularly of top-down GTA clones, they don't sell well", explains Marcinkowski. "I found that out way too late, and I thought Maniac wouldn't be a hit." His publisher was initially equally buoyant too. "But then they studied the market and stopped being so hyped. That's how it felt as we got close to release. The wishlist count wasn't very high.".

Industry observers note that "I was expecting 10,000 [copies sold]," Marcinkowski tells me. "I actually started making another game two months before Maniac came out because I thought I'd go broke." But then the game debuted, and early worries proved unfounded. It sold more than 100K copies, comfortably blowing past its maker's modest expectations, putting it in the top one percent of games released on Steam.

Recent findings suggest that it's a surprise success story built on the foundations of Marcinkowski's youth, and as we chat about GTA, he reveals he's less keen on Rockstar's modern games, which lack that classic gameplay drive. "I always liked the counter-culture side of GTA, which is why I put so much of it into Maniac," he elaborates. "GTA 6 seems to have become pop culture, so it's lost its appeal for me." Marcinkowski's heart, it seems, is old-school.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Why employees are ‘habit hugging’ at work

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after new tools and processes have been introduced.
  • If you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after new tools and processes have been introduced.
  • Habit hugging may be a sign of insecurity, or a form of self-preservation — finding stability and control in a working world that feels increasingly unfamiliar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after new tools and processes have been introduced. Habit hugging may be a sign of insecurity, or a form of self-preservation — finding stability and control in a working world that feels increasingly unfamiliar. A new report by online learning platform TalentLMS, based on a survey of 1,500 US employees who had received training on a new tool, technology, process, or way of working in the previous 12 months, found that 65% of respondents noted letting go of an old habit is harder than learning a new one. And only 41% consistently used a new way of working after they were trained on it. Meanwhile, 42% admitted they still used tools or processes their managers believed had been replaced. Multiple industries are evolving and being disrupted by AI. Habit hugging could be a response to the pressure employees feel to continually adapt as everything changes around them. As uncertainty grows both inside and outside the office, sticking to what you know may offer a little comfort. There’s a tension between employers demanding adaptability and employees being expected to maintain productivity throughout that change: The report found that 48% of respondents felt rushed to adopt new ways of working. Employers aren’t necessarily helping their workforce overcome their old habits when they expect them to adopt new systems without slowing down or making mistakes. That pressure may also make employees reluctant to admit they’re struggling. The report found that 45% of respondents had avoided questioning a new way of working because they didn’t want to appear resistant. Among those who continued to use, or fell back on, old ways of working, 22% said they feared making mistakes or looking slow. When workplaces demand this constant adaptation without creating the space for it, employees might prefer to stick to what they know. Sixty percent said their workplace prioritized results over the process of getting them, while just 41% said they felt they were given room to be less productive while learning something new. There may also be a question of trust. Employees who have seen workplace initiatives and technologies come and go may be reluctant to embrace the latest change, particularly if they aren’t convinced it will last. They may prefer to future-proof themselves by leaning on the skills and systems they already know, rather than investing time in learning a new tool that could be forgotten about in six months. That reluctance could be costing employers: The report found that 29% of employees said their organization was investing in tools they’d stopped using. But habit hugging isn’t necessarily an outright rejection of change. The report found that 73% of respondents mixed old and new ways of working to get the job done, suggesting employees may be finding ways to adapt without abandoning familiar routines altogether. Rather than blindly embracing the latest systems, people may be finding their own ways of adapting to a future nobody is sure of.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A veteran storm chaser has weighed in on Grand Theft Auto 6’s hurricanes, saying they are “pretty realistic” compared to his usual chases.

According to recent reports, back before Grand Theft Auto 6 was released, fans eagerly anticipated what Rockstar Games had up their sleeves for different features. One of the most-talked-about features pre-launch was the weather.

With Florida – sorry, Leonida – having some pretty extreme weather shifts, replicating that in-game seemed like a major task. Rockstar ultimately confirmed that the game would have the “most advanced” weather system to date. That means having torrential rainstorms, hurricanes, and massive waves hitting players.

Sources indicate that the hurricanes, though, don’t appear to unlock until you’ve completed a Strangers and Freaks mission in Lake Leonida with Freddie Gibbs, as he asks you to stay inside his doomsday bunker with him. It doesn’t have any bearing on the story, bar the latest weather, which you can choose to deal with.

Veteran storm chaser Reed Timmer – who starred in the TV show Storm Chasers – weighed in on that exact part of the game.

In posting a video of the hurricane effects, Timmer noted that it was “pretty realistic for a hurricane chase,” and added that he had gone “chasing a hurricane.”.

It has been revealed that timmer’s video put a focus on how trees reacted to the intense wind gusts, as well as how much vehicles struggled to deal with it too. “You can really see the wind here,” he stated at one point while driving an excavator. “Look at that!”.

Chasing a hurricane in GTA6 #stormchasinThis looks pretty realistic for a hurricane chase pic.twitter.com/SF91VXy2hm.

As noted, you can opt to leave Freddie’s bunker and go out in the new weather, just like Timmer did, or you can ride it out from inside.

Choosing the latter option will frustrate either Jason or Lucia, depending on who you complete the mission with, seeing as you won’t contact them for a few in-game days.

When you complete GTA 6’s story, you will unlock a cheat code that allows you to cycle through weather systems. Activating a cheat will remove your ability to unlock trophies and achievements, but it provides some fun.

Elsewhere, a birdwatching expert has weighed in on GTA 6’s wildlife, seeing as they finally found all the birds in the game.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Here's how to complete Freddie's mission and unlock hurricanes in GTA 6.
  • To unlock hurricanes in GTA 6, you must discover Freddie's side mission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, to unlock hurricanes in Grand Theft Auto 6, you must find and befriend Freddie, a prepper (and rapper) living in a hidden bunker. Complete Freddie's side mission, and the weather is sure to turn foul, though your chances of witnessing a hurricane first-hand depend on the mission's final choice.

Here's how to complete Freddie's mission and unlock hurricanes in GTA 6.

To unlock hurricanes in GTA 6, you must discover Freddie's side mission. First, visit the mysterious, unnamed, high-security compound in North Leonard County, just northwest of Lake Leonida. Approach the front gate on the south side, and a voice coming from the speakers will ask you to leave. Don't try to climb the fence; you'll be electrocuted!

Instead, walk north to the containers. There seems to be a gap beneath the orange container; use the bulldozer to push it aside and enter the tunnel below.

As soon as you emerge from the tunnel, use focus mode to see where the mines are. They'll appear as small red dots on the ground. You can shoot them, but it's much quicker to check their positions with focus mode and run past (if you don't hold a weapon, your focus won't deplete). Try to walk across rooftops, crates, and rubble as much as you can.

Recent findings suggest that A bit further ahead, to the left, you'll see drones being released from a bunker. If you shoot the first drone and hurry up, you'll likely have enough time to reach the bunker (but if not, halt for a moment and shoot the next drone as well). Once there, try to open the bunker's front door to meet Freddie.

Freddie notes he'll improve his defenses, and he'll text once he's done so you can try to break in again. You must wait a few in-game days to get Freddie's text. Leave through the front gate — the mines and drones have been disabled.

Once you've received his message, return to the compound to retest Freddie's defenses. The tunnel you used before is now blocked, so you must find another way in. To break into Freddie's compound, find the tall tower north of the fence. Climb up (one level above the ground floor is high enough) and jump onto the shed on the other side of the fence.

It has been revealed that go to the bunker while evading the mines and drones like you did the first time — beware that there will be more of each, though. You'll get an electric shock when you try the bunker's front door, but don't worry; Freddie will let you into the bunker immediately after.

In a recent development, after hanging out with Freddie for a while, you'll receive a hurricane warning. Freddie will give you a choice: stay in the bunker or leave.

Sources indicate that hurricanes should be unlocked as a permanent random weather event no matter your choice, but if you don't want to risk missing out on a guaranteed GTA 6 hurricane experience, the best choice is to leave Freddie's bunker. In both scenarios, Freddie will give you money (up to $10,000 depending on the chapter), and you can take his standout vehicle, Freddie's Dubsta.

According to recent reports, if you're just getting started in GTA 6, we have plenty of guides to help you live the high life in Leonida. Check out our GTA 6 beginner guide to get a grasp of the basics and our tips for what to do first, recommendations for the best ways to make money fast, and an explainer for how to keep stolen weapons and cars to make the most of your free time.

It has been revealed that our selection of GTA 6 guides includes help for things like how to steal the Phoenix in "Unwanted Attention" and whether you should defuse Mandy, too. There's a set of explainers for GTA 6's more open-ended side activities, like how to rob the Exotic Animal Front and where to find tree effigies for the Skunk Ape mission, and we've got all the GTA 6 cheat codes. You'll have to put in some effort before you can use those, though.

How job hunting became an expensive cash suck

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s an expense that’s easy to overlook when talking about the cost of living: getting and keeping a job. We tend to think of work as the thing that pays the bills, but commuting and the other costs associated with it come with a price tag of their own. In a recent TikTok video posted in October, content creator Char shared that she had just had to quit her job because she could no longer afford the commute. Char, who lives in the UK, said the amount of money she used to spend on a full tank of fuel now only filled her car halfway. And with fuel prices showing no sign of easing, she said, the commute was only going to get more expensive. “I can’t afford to keep driving to work,” Char said. “I can’t afford to live. Something has to give.”  And right now, she decided, that something was her job. She would have to search for a position closer to home. In the comments, people shared they had been in a similar position recently, also highlighting how everything else had hit them financially, such as grocery prices and rent. Commuting costs are also affecting people looking for work. Some job seekers have shared online how the expense of traveling to interviews is becoming difficult to manage. One creator said in a recent TikTok that she can no longer afford the job hunt. “Assuming you get past the 12,000 rounds of phone screens and Zooms, and you are invited to an on-site interview, what if you don’t have the money to commute?” she said. Compound that with the fact many are interviewing at several different companies at once, she said, and the costs quickly rack up. The costs aren’t necessarily limited to getting from A to B. Job seekers may also need to pay for childcare, buy appropriate clothes, or cover other expenses associated with making a good impression. For those who have been unemployed for some time, and have to interview in person several times, they can easily end up hundreds of dollars out of pocket. An Indeed/Harris Poll survey found that 84% of job seekers had spent money attending an in-person interview. Of those who had spent money, 30% said they spent at least $100 on their most recent interview. Meanwhile, a 2026 Monster survey of 1,005 employed US adults found that 49% of workers had turned down a job opportunity because of commuting costs or the length of the journey. More than three-quarters (76%) said current gas prices increased their financial stress, and 68% believed employers should help with commuting expenses when employees are required to work on-site. Commuting costs highlight a widening inequality between people who can afford to look for work and those who can’t. For example, job seekers with savings or financial support from their families may be better positioned to travel to interviews, pursue roles further afield, or absorb the costs of a lengthy search. For others, the price of getting to work limits the opportunities they can realistically pursue. Work is supposed to be the most obvious way of providing financial security, but that isn’t necessarily the case anymore. For some, even getting their foot in the door is becoming something they have to budget for.

More than three-quarters (76%) stated current gas prices increased their financial stress, and 68% believed employers should help with commuting expenses when employees are required to work on-site.

Commuting costs highlight a widening inequality between people who can afford to look for work and those who can’t. For example, job seekers with savings or financial support from their families may be better positioned to travel to interviews, pursue roles further afield, or absorb the costs of a lengthy search. For others, the price of getting to work limits the opportunities they can realistically pursue.

Recent findings suggest that work is supposed to be the most obvious way of providing financial security, but that isn’t necessarily the case anymore. For some, even getting their foot in the door is becoming something they have to budget for.
