#230530. Tired of GTA 6? Here's 23 lesser-known gems that might beat it at its own game

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2715 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Tired of GTA 6? Here's 23 lesser-known gems that might beat it at its own game

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You can do a lot of things in GTA 6: fishing, golfing, running, jumping, dancing, racing, roaming, shopping.
  • So what if you were in the mood for some of this stuff but away from Leonida?
  • Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch, Switch 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can do a lot of things in GTA 6: fishing, golfing, running, jumping, dancing, racing, roaming, shopping. It goes on! There's romancing, birdwatching, DIY, and even more besides. It really is an everything game. But GTA 6 isn't for everyone.

So what if you were in the mood for some of this stuff but away from Leonida? Where else might you go? Consider this the slightly tenuous set-up, as we continue a week of Not-GTA, for us to highlight some of our favourite smaller games; brilliant lesser-known titles from the last 12 months or so that, in their own special way, beat GTA 6 at its own game.

Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch, Switch 2.

It has been revealed that it's very sweet that the central, driving force of GTA 6 is the strained romance between Jason and Lucia. You are, essentially, playing a virtual matchmaker, helping these star-crossed lovers reconnect and rediscover each other after fate conspires to drive a wedge between them. But you know what's better than that? Being an actual matchmaker, matching icons on a grid and enjoying the microdose dopamine rush when you clear a line on a board.

Industry observers note that so here's Titanium Court, which goes even further: with every line cleared, you come closer to escaping a weird, 80s-core fairy castle in a game that's partly telling a story about introspective self-doubt, and partly about warring fairies. If you're getting tired of texting your virtual lover every 10 minutes, perhaps try lighting a virtual cigarette in Titanium Court, instead - I've heard it does wonders for your health.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2.

Recent findings suggest that how do you find out if you can really depend upon someone? That's a question at the heart of GTA 6. And the answer is: play Substantial Walk. There's nothing like gesturing through the window of a sound-proofed room hoping your friend or loved one will understand what two arms waggling around means. It means 'the high-pitched warbling sound plaque', obviously. Big Walk's wonderfully stripped-back world is also an antidote to GTA 6's maximal world. The silence and space in the game is absolutely the point. What will you fill it with?

It has been revealed that it's not all roof repairs and late night paintjobs. Sometimes home improvement requires more drastic measures. And in Virtue and a Sledgehammer, that's taken to violent extremes. This is a game, in developers Selkie Harbour and Deconstructeam's words, about family, tradition, and being a misfit. Where an entire town - the protagonist's childhood home - faces a total spiritual teardown. Here, a brutal sledgehammer-swinging reckoning awaits as you unearth memories - some happy, some decidedly not - through violent destruction, cutting through mechanical human facsimiles with the faces of the ones you love. It's haunting, devastating stuff; a very different kind of do-it-yourself.

Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam).

Industry observers note that you work, you sleep, and then you die. That's how it's got to be. So if you're going to toil mercilessly for the man, you can at least hope for an interesting employee. And what's more interesting than the weirdo threesome at the centre of Servant of the Lake?

Developer Rusty Lake's eponymous series returned this year with another macabre blend of point-and-click puzzling and room-escape-style adventure. And it's a corker. Perhaps not as dazzlingly experimental as some other recent entries, but it's still a delightfully grim time as you work through your three days of servitude, butlering for the oddball Vanderboom family. Beware the blood moon.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

You work, you sleep, and then you die. But! What if you dream of breaking free? Escaping the chains of drudgery? That's the starting point of Denshattack!, a Jet Set Radio-inspired adventure all about sticking it to the man. Or, more specifically, a shady megacorp trying to suppress human ingenuity, creativity, and spirit. It is, as Dom put it in their five-star Denshattack! review, a game of "anti-capitalist, pop-punk optimism", which sees you careening across a colourful Japan - as a speeding, trick-flipping train, of all things - to bring the Miraidō corporation to its knees. Stylish and satisfying.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

Umph-umph-umph-umph umph-umph-umph-umph. Oh yeah, that's the good stuff. If you want to shoot things and see them explode, and do that with immense satisfaction and a hypnotic, pulsating electronic soundtrack, this is the one. Sektori takes the feedback of a satisfying trigger pull and boils that down to its purest essence, often in spiralling, kaleidoscopic form. Hitting a full set of letters - M-I-R-A-G-E, S-E-K-T-O-R-I, etc. - summons a rainbow of action that feels like genuine ecstasy. Pure blasting and survival.

Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam), Switch, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

Umph-umph-umph-umph umph-umph-umph-umph. But this time imagine it's a disco beat. Let's breathe in the night, bask in those pulsing lights, and pretend we'll live this moment forever. Or, you know, we'll just shuffle our way through the throng of the dancefloor like a massive game of sokoban. That latter's the premise of developer Miracle Tea's Club Soko; a game about traversing an underground nightclub - one shunt at a time - to discover the secrets it holds. And it's good 'un, bringing a thinkier rhythm to its pounding beat.

Recent findings suggest that most people think of fishing as a calm escape from the hustle and bustle of daily life - that's certainly the case of GTA 6. But relaxation, I say, is for posers, which brings us to How to Fish. In developer Dazed Games' silly, chaotic physics-based fishing sim, you're given an arsenal of guns to unload upon fish and foe alike. Beware the seagulls, who have learned to love the taste of human flesh over the bounty of humble chip shops. It's great fun, especially co-operatively, so grab some pals and have a blast.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

Industry observers note that neasied, the island where Queen's Domain unfolds, might not be as dizzyingly expansive as some open-worlds, but the stuff it manages to pack into a relatively compact space is astonishing. This is a game crammed with secrets, rich with mystery; a world so dense with enigmas it's a joy to explore. There's more than a touch of FromSoftware to its broader retro-inspired combat rhythms, but there are hints of Zelda and Metroidvania too. It's one of the best games this year - full of surprise and wonder as its absurdly elaborate puzzle threads unfurl - and an extraordinary adventure.

Recent findings suggest that money too tight to mention? How about ditching the life of crime for a spot of restaurant entrepreneurialism? That's the idea behind Nivalis Night - and, actually, the life of crime is still an option. First seen in 2020 courier adventure Cloudpunk, Nivalis is a striking, sprawling cyberpunk dystopia of flying cars, neon lights, and suffocating smog that sets itself apart with its lo-fi style. And in this year's follow-up, you can finally get out of your car and live in the world. But it's not just a nifty first-person tycoon sim, it's a game of stories, and developer Ion Lands imbues its city with real warmth and humanity; a perfect accompaniment, it turns out, to all the Vangelis-like synths and sushi.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S.

Industry observers note that there's street racing and then there's developer Milestone's Screamer. It's a narrative-focused racing game which leans into a far arcadier sort of drive compared to the more realistic Grand Theft Auto. It's also got a great anime aesthetic, so you can live out any MF Ghost fantasies you have tucked away. Or maybe Initial D for the drifting aficionados among you.

Okay, fine, so it's more of a slap than a punch, but developer Double Fine's Thank You Bus Driver still packs in more violence than you'd expect from a driving sim. This game jam experiment turned full release feels a bit like a first-person Crazy Taxi as you try and get passengers to their destination before time runs out. Happy passengers means more 'thank yous', which means more time for more pick-ups, and it's a brilliantly chaotic loop.

According to recent reports, it's got bags of personality - its scrappy black-and-white doodle town and oddball passengers are a treat - and a bunch of neat hooks. Most notably, HQ intermittently imposes new rules - no talking! No toenail clipping! - which is where slaps come in. Rulebreakers need discipline if you don't want to lose your 'thank yous', so you spin around and wallop them about the chops. Just try not to drive off the road.

Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5.

Sure, Leonida's landscape holds its own kind of sunkissed beauty, but The Game Bakers has created something really special with Cairn. It might be a game focused on mountain climbing, but it's hard not to stop and admire the view whenever you reach the next plateau. As you make your way up Mount Kami, you're greeted with almost constant lovely views, some of the most gorgeous vistas released this year. Cairn is the sort of game that warrants putting the controller down and just taking the sights in for a moment or two.

Industry observers note that as a doctor of dubious repute once said, where we're going, we don't need roads! So wave goodbye to metropolitan squalor, farewell to suburban suffocation, and hello the great outdoors. Over the Hill, the follow-up to Funselektor's brilliant Art of Rally, is all about off-road roaming through the vast, untamed wilderness. It's a game of purposeful meandering and patient delights and you explore the secrets of, among other places, its starlit deserts and rolling forest hills. You'll bounce your 4x4 over rocks, crawl sluggishly up hills, and winch through squelching mud, and it's all so slow. That's deliberate though. And as the result, amid the gentle strum of soothing guitar, is a wonderfully meditative game.

Available on: PC (Steam, Epic, GOG).

There are few other games released this year that nail the ruthlessness of vehicle-to-vehicle combat like Airframe Ultra. An absolutely gorgeous battle-racer in which you take control of a bulky airframe. You can smack the daylights out of other riders with chains, bats, and other makeshift melee weapons. Failing that, ramming into people at full speed works wonders too. A gritty game that pleases the eye and nourishes the violent soul.

Life, eh? One minute it's all Leonida sunshine and motorboating, the next you're on the run. But it's how you deal with each roll of the dice that matters. And that's very much the premise of Cosmo D's wonderfully weird Moves of the Diamond Hand. It's back to the jazz-drenched, oddball world of Off-Peak City we go, this time as election day looms. The legendary Circus X has returned to town and you want a place in its show. What follows is a first-person narrative adventure that takes the tabletop RPG-inspired dice-throwing of Cosmo D's acclaimed 2022 game Betrayal at Club Low and turns it into something richer, deeper, wilder, and weirder. And yes, it's got a killer soundtrack.

Available on: PC (Steam, Epic), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.

I see you smirking, pal - cut it out. Early on in GTA 6 you're tasked with hosing off a boat in the marina. And if that scratches an unknown itch within you, PowerWash Simulator 2 has all the nozzle blasting you could hope for. Yes, it's a slightly older one, but all 2026's DLC means it still feels new. Even more grimy buildings and filthy objects are waiting for a hero with a soap dispenser, just begging for a deep clean. Is that you? Then live your dream!

Sources indicate that browsing the tourist traps and fashion emporiums for the next massive look is all well and good, but have you ever considered taking matters into your own hands? Dressmaking might not seem like the most appealing way to spend your time if you're not particularly into wearing dresses or seamstressing. (It's me, I'm that person.) However, Dressmaker and the sheer amount of clothing combinations it makes possible are a very pleasant surprise.

Weaved throughout it all is a story that sees you designing dresses for different characters and the events they're attending, then stitching your ideas to life piece by piece with tactile minigames, And you can design your own dresses too! I can only imagine GTA 6's Jason might even enjoy designing a dress or two for Lucia if he had Dressmaker on his JoyStation...

According to recent reports, creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' Johannes Zuch's Tenebrae Lux might be wowing the critics in GTA 6, but for my money this year's best game-within-a-game is Forbidden Solitaire. It's 2019 and you've stumbled upon an old copy of notorious CD-ROM adventure Forbidden Solitaire. It was pulled from the shelves amid some mysterious deaths, but that won't stop you from playing. What follows is a wonderfully creepy haunted media yarn - told across police records, press clippings, 90s local news reports, grisly photos, even a recreation of a cheesy true-crime-style mystery show - which brilliantly evokes the 90s multimedia boom with its lurid, awkward pre-rendered game-in-a-game visuals. It also, in case you're wondering, plays a damn good game of solitaire.

I like birds. I like them so much that it's at the top of my bucket list to find a Wonga Pigeon one day. So, you can imagine how I felt finding out that GTA 6 has over 60 birds to spot, alongside binoculars and a phone camera to fulfil my bird-watching dreams.

According to recent reports, before GTA 6 however, there came a lovely little multiplayer game called Flock Around developed by Friend Shaped Games that lets you explore multiple biomes while trying to snap photographs of birds from around the world and fill out your guide book. I was enamoured by its simple loop of wandering around and waiting for birds to strike a perfect pose, take selfies with them, and maybe even watching them empty their insides all over your friends. I don't think it's possible to be pooped on by a bird in GTA 6, so by default, Flock Around takes the crown as one of the best games for snapping pics of birds this year.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 might use the gorgeous relationship between Lucia and Jason to demonstrate what basic human empathy looks like in a culture that promotes instant gratification and selfishness, but Penguin Colony uses a, erm, penguin colony to highlight the existential dangers of fascism and the pervasive threat of racism and colonialism. I know which piece of social commentary I prefer.

Available on: PC (Steam, itch.io).

Sources indicate that it's not hard to have a better cleaning regimen than GTA 6's Jason: the man apparently isn't aware his nethers need a wash too. But designer Robert Yang's Rinse and Repeat's has a solution for those struggling at showertime: get someone else to help you. Rinse and Repeat is a "steamy first-person showering game ... about consent and safety" and got a remaster earlier this year as part of Yang's Radiator Forever compilation. Yang's award-winning work frequently explores queer subculture, and the NSFW compilation also contains three other games - Hurt Me Plenty, Succulent, and Stick Shift - with more to follow. Better yet, it's completely free.

Forget cracking safes in GTA 6, what about cracking the codes in a machine that seems to be, well, more than it seems? This is the hook in Inkle's TR-49, a game about a machine that once lurked in the depths of Bletchley Park's legendary codebreaking vaults, alongside the Enigma Machine. This machine works differently. It's effectively an archive you search around using codes in the format of letter-letter, number-number, hence TR-49. But the codes you use and what you find, and how you find them: that's up to you. And sure, there's probably not gold bullion on the other side of this code, but perhaps there's something even more rewarding.

GTA 6 developer shares heartbreaking story behind baby daughter’s in-game memorial

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A GTA 6 developer has thanked Rockstar Games for immortalizing his baby daughter in an in-game memorial after he and his wife lost her five months into the pregnancy.
  • Since GTA 6 released on November 19, millions of players have been exploring Leonida, uncovering hidden secrets and Easter eggs scattered throughout Rockstar’s sprawling open world.
  • However, some of the game’s most meaningful discoveries have been deeply personal tributes to the loved ones of those who spent years developing it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A GTA 6 developer has thanked Rockstar Games for immortalizing his baby daughter in an in-game memorial after he and his wife lost her five months into the pregnancy.

Since GTA 6 released on November 19, millions of players have been exploring Leonida, uncovering hidden secrets and Easter eggs scattered throughout Rockstar’s sprawling open world.

However, some of the game’s most meaningful discoveries have been deeply personal tributes to the loved ones of those who spent years developing it.

Rockstar lead game tools programmer Bradley Stone took to X to share footage of himself visiting a memorial bearing his daughter’s name, Evelyn Stone, alongside the date April 8, 2023.

“To our baby we lost at 5 months pregnancy, you have been forever memorialised and honoured,” he wrote.

“Thank you, Rockstar for giving us this place to remember our loved ones, to show this game was made by real people and thank you for all the support/care you gave me through my grief.”.

Stone explained that he and his wife had already experienced multiple miscarriages when a scan in 2023 revealed their baby had a severe case of spina bifida.

After further examinations and consultations with doctors, the couple learned that their daughter would not survive. They were left facing a medical termination, with Stone’s wife having to endure nearly 24 hours of labor.

This was the darkest moment of our lives and I cannot put into words the strength and courage my wife showed and I can only love her more for that.A few years of ups and downs and more sadness we were finally blessed with a beautiful baby girl.

It has been revealed that “We cried and held each other close as she delivered the baby,” he recalled. “The next hardest part was leaving the hospital without our baby. This still breaks me to this day.”.

It has been revealed that stone described the experience as the “darkest moment” of their lives, praising his wife’s strength and courage. He also revealed that, following several more years of ups and downs, the couple had welcomed a baby girl.

According to recent reports, “To the baby we lost, we named you Evelyn,” he wrote. “You will forever be in our hearts.”.

In a recent development, stone isn’t the only Rockstar employee whose loved ones have been immortalized in GTA 6. Fellow developer Matt Green previously revealed that his late mother, Bev, had been honored at the memorial just north of Hamlet.

While GTA 6 continues to shatter records around the world, the memorial serves as a touching reminder of the people behind the game and the loved ones they lost along the way.

Breaking: Here’s the best day to shop for travel deals—and it isn’t Black Friday or Travel Tuesday

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Black Friday may have come early this year, but the best travel deals are still to come, according to data from Skyscanner—which found the best day to find discounts on travel isn’t Black Friday or Travel Tuesday.
  • Black Friday may have come early this year, but the best travel deals are still to come, according to data from Skyscanner—which found the best day to find discounts on travel isn’t Black Friday or Travel Tuesday.
  • While Travel Tuesday generates plenty of buzz, Skyscanner analyzed billions of proprietary flight data points and found Cyber Monday was the cheapest day to book flights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday may have come early this year, but the best travel deals are still to come, according to data from Skyscanner—which found the best day to find discounts on travel isn’t Black Friday or Travel Tuesday. While Travel Tuesday generates plenty of buzz, Skyscanner analyzed billions of proprietary flight data points and found Cyber Monday was the cheapest day to book flights. That day had “the lowest average price per seat” across the five-day Black Friday-to-Travel Tuesday sales period last year, according to Skyscanner, a global travel platform. “Cyber Monday offered the lowest average fares, making it a day worth checking this year,” Lourdes Losada, Skyscanner’s director of the Americas, tells Fast Company. “Start comparing fares before the sales begin so you have a baseline, then monitor prices throughout the period. Knowing what your flight typically costs makes it easier to recognize a worthwhile offer without feeling pressured by a sale’s countdown.” However, Travel Tuesday still had plenty of standout destination-specific savings, with average flights to Fort Lauderdale, Florida; Seoul; and Honolulu dropping 28%, 24%, and 15% respectively, compared with the previous 12-month average. This is an indication that there are strong deals across the entire period. The destination that saw the largest surge in interest was Cabo San Lucas, the Mexican resort town in Baja California Sur. Searches for the location increased 444% across the full Black Friday-to-Travel Tuesday window, compared with the previous 12-month average. Other destinations that Americans searched for on Travel Tuesday included Florence, Italy (interest up 163%); Edinburgh, Scotland (up 162%); Liberia (up 158%), Hanoi, Vietnam (up 147%); and Tokyo (up 132%). Where did American travelers find the biggest Black Friday and Travel Tuesday deals? For travelers looking for savings by destination, the biggest average flight price drops were for Casablanca, Morocco (-30%); Lisbon, Portugal (-28%); Sydney (-21%); Seoul (-17%); and Honolulu (-16%). Skyscanner’s advice for shopping the deals Skyscanner recommends travelers be flexible with dates, set a price alert, stay open to fresh destinations, and check for alternative departure or arrival airports near your home and destination. The key takeaway is that travelers shouldn’t feel pressure to book on one day, since the entire five-day window provides opportunities that might otherwise be missed, according to Skyscanner. “Black Friday can bring a lot of tempting travel offers and it can also be an overwhelming time to book,” indicates Laura Lindsay, travel trends and destination expert at Skyscanner. “The key is not to rush, stay open minded and focus on the trip that works best for your budget and intends.”.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Recent findings suggest that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Creating polished visual content used to require professional equipment, editing skills and hours of manual work. Generative AI has changed that for photographers, designers, marketers and developers who build creative tools, but the results depend heavily on understanding what these systems actually do. Two techniques sit at the center of most workflows: image-to-image generation, which transforms an existing picture, and image-to-video generation, which adds motion to a still.

This article explains how both techniques work, which settings control the outcome, how several kinds of tools differ, and how to assemble a workflow with review steps, including a short code example you can run yourself. It also covers rights, authenticity and the limits of the technology. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you strategy a production.

Image-to-image resembles text-to-image, but it starts from your picture instead of pure noise. According to the Hugging Face Diffusers image-to-image guide, the initial image is encoded into latent space and noise is added to it. The model then uses the prompt and the noisy latent to predict and remove that noise, and a decoder converts the result back into an image.

Sources indicate that A single setting, usually called strength or creativity, decides how much of the original remains. In Diffusers, a higher strength gives the model more freedom, and a value of 1.0 means the starting image is largely ignored. Strength is linked to the number of denoising steps: with 50 inference steps and a strength of 0.8, the pipeline adds noise for 40 steps and then denoises for 40.

According to recent reports, the ranges above are rules of thumb, not guarantees. Models and tools respond differently, so test on your own images. The script below, adapted from the Diffusers documentation, sweeps four strength values on one source image so you can compare them side by side.

Running this requires a compatible GPU setup and model downloads, and the checkpoint name and defaults can change between library versions, so check the current documentation.

Plain image-to-image can drift from the layout you wanted. Research such as ControlNet adds spatial control to pretrained text-to-image diffusion models, with conditions such as edges, depth, segmentation and human pose. In practice, this is why many tools offer reference images, sketches, masks and pose guides on top of a prompt: they supply structure that a text prompt cannot describe precisely.

The key advantage is speed of iteration. The main limits are consistency between variations, small details such as hands and text, and the gap between a convincing concept and a usable final asset.

In a recent development, the right tool depends on what you need to control and where the output will be used. The table summarizes what each vendor’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

OpenArt’s own page describes an AI image to image generator that accepts JPEG, PNG, WEBP or HEIC files, offers a creativity slider and an optional reference image, and lets you switch between several models. Its FAQ advises uploading only images you own or have rights to use. Adobe’s Firefly page describes generative editing and video tools and states that outputs include Content Credentials, while saying its own models were trained on licensed and public-domain content. These are vendor statements, so read the current terms for the initiative you use.

In a recent development, image-to-video uses a still as the starting point for an animated scene. Most current systems extend diffusion models across time, so that a whole sequence of frames is denoised together. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequence is that the first frame strongly shapes what follows, so a clean composition and a clear subject make better clips.

For example, a still of a person walking through a rainy city can be animated with falling rain, reflections and a slow camera move. The motion instruction should describe one clear action and one camera movement rather than a long list.

Kling’s main site confirms Kling 4.0 and describes stable dynamic motion with an audio-visual experience, with image-to-video features and an API platform listed. OpenArt’s Kling 4.0 page describes how the model is offered on that platform. According to that page, videos run from 3 to 30 seconds at 720p to 1080p, you can use up to 10 keyframes and up to 15 references, and you can save a character for reuse. The page does not state pricing or generation quotas for the model. Capabilities depend on the platform that provides access and on the settings available there, so check supported inputs, output limits and cost before planning a production.

Generated motion needs checking. Warped limbs, drifting faces, flickering textures and unwanted text are common. A quick review script samples frames and reports basic file properties:.

Industry observers note that consider a small business preparing a campaign for a newly introduced skincare product. The same steps apply to any visual project.

This process reduces the effort of exploring concepts and makes it easier to test several versions of an advertisement before choosing a direction. It does not remove the need for human review.

They can be, with different priorities. Photographers can explore creative treatments, mood boards and alternative backgrounds without replacing traditional photography. Marketers can develop campaign concepts, create variations of social graphics and test promotional videos. In both cases the value comes from supporting a clear creative objective rather than adopting a tool because it is fresh.

A technique that transforms an existing image using a prompt, by adding noise to the image and then regenerating it under guidance. A strength or creativity setting controls how much of the original is kept.

Use a lower strength, a reference image or a structure condition such as edges or depth where the tool supports it.

Yes. Image-to-video tools animate a still from a motion description, though complex motion can introduce inconsistencies, so review every clip.

No. Several vendors and platforms offer video generation. Compare supported inputs, length, resolution, cost and licensing against your needs.

It depends on the tool, the plan and the rights you hold in the inputs. Read the current terms and keep records of your sources.

Recent findings suggest that image-to-image and image-to-video tools give creators a faster way to explore ideas, but they work best when you understand their controls. Strength settings decide how much of the original survives, conditioning methods preserve structure, and the starting frame shapes video. Compare hosted platforms, vendor apps and open-source libraries against your needs, build review and provenance into the workflow, and treat the output as a draft that a person checks before it ships.

#230525. I'm having a much better time in GTA 6 now I've disabled its pesky Criminal Profile pings

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1363 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

I'm having a much better time in GTA 6 now I've disabled its pesky Criminal Profile pings

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that do you think you'd enjoy invasive UI elements in real life?
  • I think it would interact with my already-questionable perception of reality, and send my neurodivergent coping mechanisms into overdrive.
  • According to recent reports, so why is it any different in GTA 6?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that do you think you'd enjoy invasive UI elements in real life? You crouch to fuss your dog, and a little ping activates in your retina, informing you that you've just earned plus-three serotonin. Your boss chews you out for coming into work 15 minutes late thanks to a traffic accident holding you up on your way to work, a notification pings: "-10 percent motivation (lasts 24 hours)". Maybe you eat a bang-up meal, flirt with a hot stranger, beat your personal best on a run - ding, ding, ding. Well done, you win at being a human.

I think it'd be tortuous. I think it would interact with my already-questionable perception of reality, and send my neurodivergent coping mechanisms into overdrive. I already see time 'in blocks', and am incapable of breaking tasks down to anything less than 15 minute chunks - I can't imagine how ill I'd get if I could begin ascribing status buffs and debuffs to those blocks, too. We're all different, of course - such is the beauty of life - but I think most people would be pushed to the point of meltdown if every action they took had a quantifiable mechanical system attached to it.

According to recent reports, so why is it any different in GTA 6? The game, after all, is the most effective simulation we've ever seen about modern life. Aside from the rampant crime sprees you can engage with, there's so much mundanity in the game it's beyond impressive: I spent the opening 10-or-so hours in the game with a very strict morning routine. I'd get up, work out, shower, feed Dolores the snake, drink a protein shake, then head to one of the local businesses to get some breakfast. Every day! I'm a busy person; I'm playing GTA 6 for fun, yes, but also as part of my job - I need to be making progress. Yet, Rockstar's invisible hand is so competently realised, so artisanally implemented, that I bow to its insistence that I live life properly and engage with all the systems suggested to me like a good little drone.

So, after being low-key brainwashed by the initial tutorialisation, it stands to reason that I'm open to Rockstar's other suggestions. And - right on cue - you get a mission early on that introduces you to what is perhaps the most hotly debated aspect of the game so far: the Criminal Profile. If you're unaware, this latest mechanic is a bit like the Honour System in Red Dead Redemption 2. It's broken down into five levels: professional, hardened, violent, psycho, and irredeemable. If you hit that final bracket, irredeemable, you can never go back: it's essentially GTA 6's criminal version of 'being cancelled', only here there are real, serious consequences that will actually ruin your life forever.

The game tracks how you behave when you're playing as both Jason and Lucia. They have separate criminal profiles. If, for example, you fudge a robbery on a cartel's pill-shipping operation and fight for your life, you can certainly kill everyone in the room - that's still fine. This is still Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar isn't trying to make you play this game like Thief or Deus Ex or something. You can go for total stealth runs, but incapacitating enemies without killing them and getting away cleanly will only grant 'professional' points. You get the same assessment if you 'go loud' and aim for the hands, knees, feet of the people trying to kill you. I am right now about 30 hours in, and every single encounter has been either 'no casualties' or 'low casualties', and I promise I've not even been trying that hard to 'be good' (and there are always settings you can change to help you out if you're struggling, too).

Industry observers note that there has been a certain amount of online discourse pointing towards this system as 'immersion ruining' or 'systematically inhibiting'. There's this idea that, in order to get a number of the game's 'good' endings, you need to play like a saint the whole way through the game. This is untrue. It's actually weighted more towards the opposite: in order to get the more nefarious ranks, you need to intentionally play like a sociopath. Wing a goon, see him lying on the floor in agony, and then go over and shoot his other kneecap? Yeah, you're going to get those unpopular purple devil points. Kick a dog in the street for no reason? Devil points. Taking a shotgun to a mall and opening fire on unarmed, un-implicated civilians? Devil points.

I'm enjoying the role-playing aspect of the game, because in my head-canon Jason and Lucia are doing what they can to survive. It may not be pretty, and I probably wouldn't want to know them in real life, but - as far as this work of fiction goes - I think playing them as criminals-on-the-run, trying to draw as little attention to themselves as possible is a great iteration of the series' core themes. I don't want to play as another Tommy Vercetti, or CJ, or Trevor. I want something different, and this game is giving it to me.

Industry observers note that "The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper," explains Michael Wiafe, writer at Rockstar, in materials shared with Eurogamer ahead of the game's release. "[They're] full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn’t necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don’t attempt to make excuses for them. What’s vital is how they resonate, no matter where you’re experiencing the game in the world." I think this demonstrates, quite well, what the Criminal Profile mechanic sets out to achieve in GTA 6: it's Rockstar saying 'these people are forced into certain situations by us, the developers, but you get to figure out how they respond to what life is giving them'.

Sources indicate that and you know what? I'm glad GTA 6 punishes you for playing like a psychopath. The world of Leonida is analogous to the real world, and things would start going wrong for you if you started attacking pedestrians randomly on the street. Other civilians and cops would start defending themselves and resisting you if you instigated a rampage of indiscriminate violence. The only time I've been victim to the devil icon in my game so far is when a Kingfisher accidentally shot out my (very expensive) windshield whilst aiming for Jason. So I kneecapped him, stole his beer, drank the whole bottle, then threw the bottle at his head. I acted like an idiot, and got treated as such. Good!

But I don't want to see that. I want to roleplay as Jason and Lucia and act as I think they would. I don't need the game telling me, like a little voice in my head, 'hm, actually, that was a pretty weird thing to do, we're going to write that down'. So I have turned the notifications off. It's a simple process: simply open Settings, and then navigate to UI, and head down to the 34/70 area and you'll see all the HUD notifications settings. I play with both Criminal Profile and Relationship settings turned off - I prefer to have all that happening in the background, ticking over as I play, rather than constantly reminding me there's some secret meter somewhere judging me for what I'm doing.

If my relationship is turning sour, I trust my instincts (and Rockstar's grounded, well-structured writing) to tell me that. Jason is getting a bit cold, Lucia doesn't want to jump my bones, like, all the time, the two aren't holding hands at every opportunity like lovesick puppies… Much like in my real-life relationships, I trust the process. And I think more people should, because the role-playing in this game is fantastic, and we've been given a real rich text to engage with. I think that the fact that certain corners of the internet are upset because they're being treated badly for being bad people is a better level of satire than anything GTA 6 has put in-game, to be honest.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving centers on gratitude, which is good for mental health, as scientific studies have proven.
  • Thanksgiving centers on gratitude, which is good for mental health, as scientific studies have proven.
  • The stress and anxiety of the holiday season can almost seem antithetical to these findings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving centers on gratitude, which is good for mental health, as scientific studies have proven. The stress and anxiety of the holiday season can almost seem antithetical to these findings. It’s hard to be zen when wondering if the local supermarket is open because you need another cup of milk for the mashed potatoes. Here’s everything you need to know about what is open and closed on Thanksgiving for those last-minute needs. We even threw in some fun facts so you can wow everyone at dinner with your wit and wisdom. Do other countries celebrate Thanksgiving? The United States is not the only country that celebrates gratitude at the end of the year. The first recorded Canadian Thanksgiving took place in 1578, which was more than 40 years before its American counterpart. In Canada, Thanksgiving takes place on the second Monday in October. In Germany, Erntedankfest, a harvest of thanks, takes place in September or October, depending on the year. In Japan, Kinro Kansha no Hi, Labor Thanksgiving Day, focuses on appreciation for workers. This celebration evolved from an ancient rice festival and takes place on November 23. In Liberia, Thanksgiving falls on the first Thursday of November. A spicy roast chicken is the main dish, not turkey. Is Thanksgiving a federal holiday? Yes. In the United States, Thanksgiving takes place on the fourth Thursday of November and is a federal holiday. Are banks open on Thanksgiving? No, most are closed for the holiday, as is the Federal Reserve. Online banking and ATMs outside branches are good alternatives. Is the stock market open on Thanksgiving? No. Even the stock market takes a day off to be grateful for capital gains. Both the Upcoming York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are closed. Is the Post Office open on Thanksgiving? Is Mail delivered? Unless you are getting your Hogwarts acceptance letter by owl, no mail will be delivered on Thanksgiving. Physical post office locations operated by the U.S. Postal Service will be closed for the holiday. Online services and self-serve kiosks are your best bet in a pinch. Are FedEx and UPS delivering on Thanksgiving? No, FedEx locations are not open and it is not delivering or picking up on Thanksgiving. Most UPS locations are also closed and the organization is not delivering or picking up. The only exception is UPS Express Critical service. Are schools open on Thanksgiving? No. The majority of schools will not be in session due to the holiday. It is always a good practice to double-check with your child’s institution. Are restaurants open on Thanksgiving? Yes. Many restaurants will be open. Some will even feature a special menu for the holiday as certain families would rather make reservations than a turkey with all the trimmings. Are retail stores open on Thanksgiving? Only some retail stores will be open on Thanksgiving. Walmart, Target, REI, Kohl’s, Dick’s Sporting Goods, and Home Depot are just some of the chains that will be closed. It is probably safer to focus on turkey instead of shopping on Thanksgiving. On Black Friday, however, all bets are off. Are pharmacies open on Thanksgiving? Some pharmacies will remain open on Thanksgiving. For instance, more than 4,000 Walgreens locations will be open. It is best to double-check your favorite location before you head out so you avoid getting headaches, even if they are just metaphorical ones. Are grocery stores open on Thanksgiving? Only some grocery stores are open on Thanksgiving. Do not go to Costco, Trader Joe’s, Sam’s Club, Aldi or Publix for last-minute meal supplies as you will find closed doors. Kroger says stores will be open until 4 p.m. Whole Foods says most stores are open with modified hours, so check your local location. What television specials are happening on Thanksgiving? Since 1924, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been delighting spectators with its significant balloons, floats, and musical acts. This year marks its 100th iteration (No parades took place from 1942 to 1944 because of World War II)). However, the parade will be postponed for the first time in its history. New York City is under a high-wind warning due to a nor’easter. New balloons joining in on the milestone celebration include Bluey, Hello Kitty, Joe Cool and Woodstock, and Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey. Natasha Bedingfield, Devo, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, Mckenna Grace, Megan Moroney, Indigo Girls, JoJo, Wyclef Jean, Queen Latifah, Leslie Odom Jr., Anthony Ramos, Smash Mouth, and Teddy Swims are just some of the performers lending their talents to the parade route. One controversial change is a single 10-minute Broadway medley featuring performers from nine Broadway demonstrates. Historically, several shows have been able to perform their own numbers. The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is broadcast on NBC on Saturday, November 28, from 8:30 a.m. to 12 noon, across all time zones. It will also be available to stream on Peacock.

#230522. Breaking: "I'm betting on the sickos" - Signet City plans to 'expand the scope of RPGs' by drawing on the success of Citizen Sleeper

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2527 w)

Breaking: "I'm betting on the sickos" - Signet City plans to 'expand the scope of RPGs' by drawing on the success of Citizen Sleeper

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I last spoke to Citizen Sleeper creator Gareth Damian Martin, it was on the eve of Citizen Sleeper 2's release.
  • "I feel a certain responsibility that comes with success," Damian Martin - also known by their studio name Jump Over the Age - told me at the time.
  • They wanted the definition of RPGs to be "expanded", to make them as varied as "rich and varied" as tabletop RPGs can be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I last spoke to Citizen Sleeper creator Gareth Damian Martin, it was on the eve of Citizen Sleeper 2's release. Like its predecessor, the game was a critical hit, cementing Damian Martin's reputation as one of the most successful independent game developers around. But they weren't content. They wanted to do more, to push more, to stretch the idea of what a role-playing video game could be.

"I feel a certain responsibility that comes with success," Damian Martin - also known by their studio name Jump Over the Age - told me at the time. "I feel lots of things about this medium, and I feel if I'm in the one percent of indie developers - and the even smaller percent of solo developers - who manage to make something and have that thing be successful, then I have responsibility towards putting things into the industry and into the world that contribute somehow to whatever I think the industry should be doing.".

They wanted the definition of RPGs to be "expanded", to make them as varied as "rich and varied" as tabletop RPGs can be. Citizen Sleeper was a step towards realising that goal but even it had limitations, which is why Damian Martin has returned to take things a step further with their next game Signet City. Confirmed during this year's somewhat samey-feeling Summer Game Fest, it's a startlingly original work.

Industry observers note that signet City was enigmatic. Revealed in a cinematic trailer, it was black and white, bleak, thick-lined, smoggy, and dirty; choked in industrial decay and brimming with post-punk non-conformance. It was also first-person, a notable change for Damian Martin, whose games have, up until now, been zoomed out and abstracted. Most eye-catching of all, though, was the descriptor "fungalpunk" - a game in which we'd play as a parasite in someone's mind. As far as expanding the scope of RPGs goes: "100 percent that is exactly what I'm trying to do here," Gareth Damian Martin tells me now.

We talk in a video call in the immediate aftermath of Signet City's announcement - apologies for not writing this until Not-GTA Week, though what an opportunity that presented - and Damian Martin is as calm and eloquent and thoughtful as ever, nestled in a compact office decorated with collages of their current influences. This room looked different when we spoke about Citizen Sleeper 1, looked different when we spoke about Citizen Sleeper 2, and it looks different again now. Damian Martin is a visual person, as someone with a visual design background would be.

It has been revealed that with Signet City only just announced, questions abound. The announcement trailer doesn't reveal much (not much has come out since, either), but we do know it takes place in the North of England in the 80s. It's a setting I'm not sure we've ever had in games, and one that's woefully overlooked in entertainment in general, barring BBC TV highlights like Our Friends in the North and Boys from the Blackstuff, which Damian Martin directly references. We know there are themes like industrial decay, welded as they are to that time and place. But there's been no talk of how the game plays, or what being a parasite in someone's mind means.

Recent findings suggest that after speaking with Damian Martin, I've got a much better idea. But first, to the beginning. Signet City is an idea they've had floating around their head for a very long time. This was the game they pitched to their publisher Fellow Traveller after Citizen Sleeper 1 came out, but decided to hold in favour of making Citizen Sleeper 2 - a decision driven partly by a desire "to build myself a bigger platform" to launch a fresh game idea from. The idea originated in a very unexpected place: the musician Sting. Damian Martin was doing theatre design for Sting's musical show The Last Ship before they became a full-time game-maker (go back even further in Damian Martin's life and you'll find a degree in puppetry there). They had to research Newcastle in the 1980s because of it. The Last Ship is about Sting's upbringing in Wallsend, a town near Newcastle, in the wake of a shipyard being closed there - the town's source of sustenance. And it was while working on the project that the 80s imprinted on Damian Martin's mind.

"I was looking at these pictures of these massive gleaming ships hanging over the top of little terraced houses," they say, "and this conflict between time periods and ideas of society, and I remember thinking at the time: that was science-fiction somehow. When you look at those images, it could be a spaceship; that ship that's being built in Newcastle might as well be a spaceship, especially science-fiction of the 80s - a lot of it was about that.

It has been revealed that "It just stuck in my brain and I started to work up this fictional 1980s British city that would be in that period of de-industrialisation and social change," they continue. "But would be based on a completely different kind of industrial background and have this weird kind of fungalpunk technology layered into it. So that's been sitting around in my head for almost 10 years slowly accruing material and reference points and things.".

It has been revealed that fungalpunk: there's that word again, but what does it mean? I've heard of cyberpunk and steampunk, not that I could tell you easily what they mean, but I've never heard of fungapunk - I don't think anyone has. Thankfully, in this case, it's fairly literal. "You are fungal in a very true sense," Damian Martin states. You are a fungal parasite and there are themes of decay and reinvigoration, things fungi are closely tied to. One of the phrases Damian Martin has been using as a north star for the project - something they do on all of their projects - is the idea of being "a fungal superhero", which makes me giggle. I've definitely not heard that before either.

It's an idea inspired by a 1989 Japanese film called Tetsuo: The Iron Man - about a salary man who's slowly turning into metal - that Damian Martin adores. "I love it so much," they say. "It's an amazing movie, a beautiful movie, and really strange. And so I wanted to do something that was in that vibe. The way that that film commits to the idea of a body becoming metal and the visceral kind of strangeness of that. I wanted to do something that was about humans and becoming fungal; which we already are, we already have lots of bits of bacteria and fungal nail infections - we are multitudes.".

The punk side of the equation is, again, fairly literal. It refers to the post-punk cultural and musical scene at the time. The scene is often overshadowed by the brasher, more aggressive punk movement, but it's one that's just as anti-establishment, albeit in perhaps in a deeper, darker, more nihilistic way. Think Joy Division referencing novelist JG Ballard in its songs, for example. "Post-punk was this engagement with structural politics and transgressive fiction and all kinds of interesting big ideas getting into pop culture through music," Damian Martin says.

According to recent reports, now watch the game's trailer again; you can feel all these things oozing through it. The aesthetic, the music, the setting. There are also big clues - although they're not obvious - about how the game plays. We see the start of a character called Sid's story in the trailer, who's one of the hosts we can inhabit in the game. We choose an area of the city we want to play in, then drop into a person's head who lives or operates there. And in Sid's case, she wakes up in a river just as we - the parasite - wake in her mind. Twins!

In a recent development, we control Sid as we would a character in another first-person game - Dishonored or Skyrim are two examples Damian Martin uses - and we see a bit of this in the trailer. What we don't see are any other mechanics, which are, once more, dice rolls related to skills, as in Citizen Sleeper. In order to do something in the world that isn't insignificantly easy, we need to roll a dice and add modifiers to see if we can achieve it.

It has been revealed that "So the way it works is you drop into someone's head for the day. Let's say we drop into this worker's head for the day and we want to get to a certain part of the city, and let's say we need to kick down a door to get there," notes Damian Martin. "Well, we're going to have to make this character really angry to get them to kick down that door, so we're going to maybe get them in an argument with some other fellow workers, and maybe we're going to choose to provoke that argument and then they'll get really angry. Then that will have narrative effects, but also it will have mechanical effects in the sense of, like, okay, now we have a modifier that makes physical strength more powerful, so we can do these physical strength actions.".

Skills are tied to a person's emotions, intriguingly, and your job as the parasite is to find things that affect these emotions so you can amplify them and increase your chances of achieving things. Then at the end of the day, all of that emotion gets "extracted out" and becomes a resource you can permanently improve your host's skills with. "So you start to adjust each of your hosts in a direction you think will be helpful for you to do what you need each day in these hub locations," Damian Martin explains. But this has consequences. Push someone towards angry actions and they'll become a more angry person, understandably. "And that will shape their future even when you're no longer controlling them.".

Industry observers note that which begs the question: what exactly does a parasite need to do? What is a parasite's objective in the game? This is an answer Damian Martin isn't quite ready to give, though they do their best to attempt it. "You have your own objectives as a parasite," they say. "You don't have an objective like: this is your mission, parasite. But there are some bigger offers coming to you through your sensorium, through your experience of voices and attractions and tastes and smells, that are leading you in different places as a parasite. That's your objective, to grow and gain power, although to what end you don't initially know.".

It's in this parasitical difference Signet City starts to stand apart. For starters, it's just appealing weird to be a parasite, though as Damian Martin muses, aren't we often parasites in relation to characters in tabletop role-playing games? "We push them around; sometimes we talk for them and sometimes we listen to them; sometimes we use our name and sometimes we use their name." Here, it's simply out in the open. "I wanted to create an RPG where I acknowledged and then also played that into the fiction," they say.

Being in a thing in someone's mind allows a host character autonomy, to a degree, so they can have their own motivations and stories and struggles besides yours. They don't have to be thoughtless mannequins awaiting our direction. Dropping into their minds allows us to drop straight into a tense scenario. "Stories for me that are very exciting in fiction and literature are stories about people who are in it," Damian Martin says. "They're in the situation already, they're in the shit, they're having to deal with everything.".

The ability to read their minds also lets us know them more intimately than we know characters in other games, who usually, you know, need to speak to us in order for us to understand them. It also circumvents the need for an NPC to suddenly and unnaturally open up to you about their lives, the first moment they meet you, and to provide you with "a neatly packaged challenge". That's not needed here. "The core relationships of the game are actually between you and your hosts," Damian Martin says.

Recent findings suggest that there's a layer that exists on top of the character's thoughts where the parasite lives and functions - a layer of feelings and emotions and sensory reactions to a world outside. A hopefully quite bizarre and alien layer, which presents challenges of its own, because how do you describe the experiences of a parasite in someone's mind? "What does it feel like to be a parasite and how do I make that comprehensible to a human?" Damian Martin wonders. They are good questions I can't wait to experience the answers to.

Recent findings suggest that but when will that be? There's no release date yet, and when we talked in the summer, Signet City was only halfway through development. It was unveiled early partly to make sure people understood it wasn't Citizen Sleeper 3, and partly because people could probably use some time to sit with the idea for a bit and digest it. "We can't just drop it all on everyone's heads," Damian Martin indicates, "because I think the potential for it being misunderstood or just ignored is high.".

Recent findings suggest that and that's a telling admission for a project which has been characterised by Damian Martin multiple times as a risk - as even "the biggest swing I have ever taken". They seemed genuinely nervous about announcing it, though some of those nerves were subsiding by the time we talked. They're not entirely gone, mind you. There's a lingering awareness that Signet City is new and different enough that people might not gel with it, though that's the price of pushing at boundaries, I suppose.

In a recent development, "What worries me more," Damian Martin says, "is have I still got it? Am I able to produce things that are appealing and exciting to people just based on my own tastes and obsessions and interests? When it comes to announcing something like Signet City, that's what makes me really nervous - more than industry, more than money, more than anything. Is this actually interesting?".

Industry observers note that of course, it's easy for me to say they shouldn't worry. It's exciting when a game blares as loudly and uniquely as Signet City did during Summer Game Fest, though that is obviously no guarantee it'll find an audience. But I think it will. I'm convinced there are more people like me who it will appeal to. Gareth Damian Martin is betting on it. "I'm betting on the sickos," they say. "The thing I've learned is that my obsessions are sticky and they stick to other people, and I think there's something in art where we really like to be tourists in other people's obsessions - that's a fun place to be. That's what I'm hoping for.".

#230520. At last, I've finally played Faraway, an enigma I've been waiting 16 years to see

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2289 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

At last, I've finally played Faraway, an enigma I've been waiting 16 years to see

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for 16 years I've been watching the skies.
  • Faraway is one of those wonderfully cludged together childhood words, like "nonesuch".
  • Okay, Faraway came with one other bit of info I could cling to at the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for 16 years I've been watching the skies. It was 16 years ago, back in the first giddy rush of smartphone gaming, that I saw a 30-second trailer for a game set in space. It was a game about a comet, hurtling through the unknown. It wasn't clear what you'd do in this game, whether you'd control the comet itself or the space it moved through. It wasn't clear if this was some kind of arcade game, or a new spin on the endless runner, or even just a kind of cosmic sandbox. All I had was the comet and a name: Faraway. Faraway! I was captivated.

Faraway is one of those wonderfully cludged together childhood words, like "nonesuch". Where is the edge of the galaxy? Oh, it's faraway. Where is the edge of the universe? Oh, there's nonesuch thing.

Okay, Faraway came with one other bit of info I could cling to at the time. It was being made by Steph Thirion, a musician and designer and, I sensed, many other things too. At the time Faraway was announced I'd just played his game Eliss, which was an early smartphone hit. In the absence of any more information on Faraway itself, I had to make do with that. Maybe Faraway would be a bit like Eliss?

Eliss itself, though? Oh, boy. This thing is beautiful, frantic, strange, compelling and indescribable. And think what that means, just for a second, for something to be both compelling and indescribable. I am driven to do these things, but I don't really know what these things are. I'm prodding little bits of colour around, maybe planets, maybe molecules? I am combining them, gathering them, turning them into something greater together than they are by themselves?

Last week I spoke to Thirion - as for why, well, we will get to that - and at the start I asked him about Eliss, about how it felt to make a game that was so hard to put into words, and if he actually had any words for it himself.

Recent findings suggest that "I love that question," he laughs. "I guess I would say that for Eliss, it was all about that interaction of moving things, moving those little circles with each of your fingers individually." He pauses, thinking back. "It's not something I had envisioned. I was programming, and I was basically testing touch controls because I was trying to build a different game. But then I was playing with that [stuff]. I was like: that feels really nice. Can I build a game around that? So I guess there is something beyond language about that interaction. I was attracted to it in that way. It wasn't rational. It was a feeling. It feels good.".

It's both thrilling and slightly melancholic to think back to the days of Eliss. Apps were in ascendence, but nobody fully understood them yet. There weren't yet consultants or established monetisation pathways. There wasn't even much agreement on the best ways to approach the touchscreen. Eliss and other weird, memorable, hard-to-talk-about games were all part of this Cambrian explosion. You'd get up in the morning and check socials and there was a new game everyone was enthusing about. There was a new world to get lost in.

"I would say that's true even outside of mobile," Thirion tells me. "Just indies in general. There was a lot of excitement going around and a lot of eyeballs. What are people gonna think about next?" He takes a long breath. "It felt like there's a lot of opportunity for newly introduced things and new ideas, and people were excited about that. Everything was set up for innovation. It felt like I was part of something.".

In a recent development, this is the world that Faraway and its comet first emerged from, streaking across a night sky in which any kind of discovery felt possible. "The real genesis was actually just before Eliss," Thirion indicates. "I was really spending a lot of time thinking about a possible career in video games. I was an interaction designer and programmer doing interactive experiences, mostly for advertising.

Industry observers note that "And for some reason, the iPhone was the thing that made me think I could do something on my own, and what I'd like to do is probably video games. So I was I was thinking a lot about that, maybe obsessively, to the point where there was a night that I was in the countryside in France and just looking at the stars and thinking: it would be great to have a video game where you can fly in the sky that I'm looking at, in this 2D firmament, right? That was it.".

Sources indicate that the next step towards Faraway came at GDC in 2010, with a call for games that could be controlled with a single button. "I started prototyping," Thirion notes. "I tried a few things, and I had this idea of using this kind of physics-y thing about swinging around stars. It actually worked pretty swiftly.".

Then? Sixteen years pass. What was happening during this time?

It has been revealed that it's a long answer with, perhaps, a short answer buried inside it. Let's deal with the long answer first.

"It's not like I worked 16 years on this game," Thirion laughs. He explains that the first prototype was begun in 2010 for the GDC one-button competition. It was playable by March. "That was basically at the beginning," he says. "I was like: This is a very simple game, and I'm just going to put it out in a couple months.".

According to recent reports, and after that? "I started to have greater ambitions, and then life happened," he says. He didn't work on the game for seven years, and then Annapurna Interactive found him and asked him to return to Faraway, offering support. "And so, after that, the journey was to turn [the game] into an audiovisual experience.

Recent findings suggest that "And so I started doing an audiovisual experience, but it was still aesthetically like Ellis: low-resolution pixel art. I had the ambition of taking it to a different language. I basically wanted to make the jump from procedural low-resolution to procedural infinite resolution!" He ended up with a very smooth, almost vector-like aesthetic. It looks beautiful, but it came at a price. "That took a lot of effort," he says. "Also to make it performant? That required a rewrite of the game into a completely upcoming engine. It was a new language for me as well, so I had to learn this new language.".

Recent findings suggest that all of this is extremely convincing, as are a hundred other bumps in the road. It makes sense. I've written about games for twenty years, and my sense is that game development is hard, and that it takes time.

Sources indicate that but there's something else Thirion says. And this makes me wonder if part of the truth as to why Faraway took so long to make is actually a lot simpler, and a lot more human.

"I was thinking a lot about Tetris," Thirion says. "I had just started making video games, and I thought a lot about Tetris because it's a very simple rule set that seems to be compelling whether you're two hours in or 1000 hours in, right? And that's like kind of a rare thing.

It has been revealed that "And at the time we were talking about: are game's art and so on. And I was like, man, to me, Tetris is art. It does something almost impossible. At least now I look at it and I think it does something almost impossible. But at the time, I was like, well, why are games growing in complexity and quantity instead of staying simple and going deep? And so, I was really asking myself the question: where can I find that balance of just being compelling at any skill level with a very minimal rule set, and that kind of took me into this rabbit hole of experimentation.".

It's hard for me not to sympathise with this. Thirion had worked on something for a very short period of time, and he'd found something that felt - well, that felt kind of eternal, boundless in there. A comet swinging through space with one touch controls! What could be more pleasing, more engaging than that? But with that came a lot of challenges. It wasn't just a question of what to add. Adding things would be easy. It was how to create a deep experience that didn't overburden the whole idea and make you lose sight of its simplicity. Put like that, 16 years doesn't seem like a very long time at all.

According to recent reports, that's his journey, anyway. As for mine? Well, 16 years is a lot of time if you aren't a comet. I continued writing about games. I got married. I had a daughter. My daughter grew up and went to primary school and is now at secondary school. The whole games industry transformed and then transformed again and is transforming again now. I started learning to swim!

And throughout all this, every few years I would email Thirion and ask if he was ready to talk yet, whether he was ready to talk about Faraway and whether his comet was still blazing somewhere in some private night sky.

In a recent development, earlier this year I looked him up once more and saw a new trailer. It was short again, and there was the comet I had seen all those years ago. And then, at the end, there was a date. A release date. That comet was finally swinging by the earth.

And so a few weeks ago I loaded up a game I had been waiting to play for 16 years and which I realised, as I paged through the early screens, that I still knew absolutely nothing about. Well. Do you want to hear about it? Or would you rather discover it for yourself?

In a recent development, I would rather you discover it for yourself. But if you don't want to, listen:.

In a recent development, faraway is a game about a comet. The comet is racing through space, and you are the comet, even if you only control it indirectly. Touch a button - there is only one button - and you can bind the comet to the gravity of a nearby star. Keep your finger pressed down on the button and you will remain gravitationally bound, which means you can use stars to adjust your course, your trajectory, your speed. Let go of the button and you're off again. Off into the depths of space. And out there, upcoming stars await.

Industry observers note that from this simple interaction, Faraway builds a constellation of challenges that I find both simple to understand and - yes - incredibly difficult to adequately put into words. I'm not going to tell you too much, because I really want you to play this thing, but Faraway at its core is a bit like sewing, a bit like driving, a bit like counting and making shapes and a bit like desperately trying to stay alive. That's it. It's beautiful and serene, but it's also desperate. It's abstract and reliable and I find it extremely moving to play.

Sources indicate that more than anything, I think I love the feel of it. The steady arc of the comet bends and flexes beneath you as you push and hold the button. There's a thrilling sense of just about bending something elemental to your will. There's beauty to be found in timing your escape from an orbit, and the orbit paths themselves, when you press and hold the button and new trajectories announce themselves, have a Spirograph delight to them. Does it really matter what you do in a game when it has stuff like this in it?

Recent findings suggest that now, I am weird, and I spend a lot of my time on Earth thinking about the wilds of space and the vast distances and the places we will never get to see and all the things that are so hostile to life that we wouldn't survive a second in their presence. I think about the Wow Signal and the Great Attractor and Tabby's Star and all of that beautiful, terrifying stuff. It calms me down. It puts my own problems in perspective. It's probably the closest thing I get to any kind of religious observance.

And Thirion thinks about this stuff too. I know because, after 16 years, I asked him. "It really resonates with me," he says. "I do spend a lot of time thinking about [the universe]. I don't know why there is anything at all, right? And the fact that we can never answer that question, and the fact that there are many questions that we'll probably never be able to answer.

It has been revealed that "But I also spend a lot of time looking at the clouds and looking at the grass and how the light hits the drops of water. There's so much beauty. We're given so much beauty by the universe, and we're so lucky.

"And the game comes out of that a little bit. I don't know exactly what the game is about, but maybe you could interpret it as: why am I here? Why is life so short? Why is life so long?".

He laughs. "I often ask myself: why is there anything at all? And how is it so beautiful?".
