#230519. Stop scheduling meetings over lunch

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2127 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Stop scheduling meetings over lunch

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ever wonder what happened to the front porch?
  • The front porch used to play an important role in everyday life.
  • Recent findings suggest that there was no single moment when the front porch disappeared.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever wonder what happened to the front porch? The front porch used to play an vital role in everyday life. Neighbors who weren’t necessarily close friends saw each other, stopped to talk, and maintained a sense of community. Then daily life moved indoors. Air-conditioning made staying inside more comfortable, television pulled families into the living room, and backyard patios offered more privacy so you didn’t have to say “hi” to the overly talkative neighbor. There was no single moment when the front porch disappeared. It just gradually became less central to the way people connected, and faded away. The lunch break is headed in the same direction. Technology has made it possible to collaborate across locations and time zones, while AI is helping work move faster than ever. But constant connectivity has also weakened the boundaries around the workday. An open hour at noon can swiftly become another meeting or a chance to catch up on work. Peer pressure plays a role too. Employees see colleagues and leaders eating at their desks or scheduling meetings over lunch with a polite, “Sorry, it was the only free time I could find.” Eventually, skipping lunch becomes an unwritten expectation rather than an individual choice. And when that behavior is rewarded with recognition and career growth, the expectation becomes even harder to challenge. Yet lunch is one of the few natural opportunities during the workday to step away and connect with colleagues without an agenda. It also gives employees a chance to decompress, take a walk, and mentally reset before tackling the rest of the day. Leaders who want sustainable performance should make sure that opportunity doesn’t disappear. 5 ways to protect lunch breaks  You don’t have to mandate how employees spend lunch. Some people want to eat with colleagues. Others prefer to take a walk, run an errand, or simply be alone. The point is to create a culture where stepping away feels like a normal choice. And it requires looking at the signals your workplace sends about availability, performance, and connection. 1. Create space that can’t automatically become another meeting If every open block on a calendar is considered schedulable, lunch will always be at risk. Consider establishing meeting-free windows during the day so employees have protected time to recharge. Adapt that approach for global and frontline teams instead of assuming the same time works for everyone. Employees across time zones and operating environments may need different windows, but the principle is the same: Build recovery into the work day. 2. Model the behavior you want  Culture is a collection of the norms, values, and behaviors that employees see around them every day. And nothing is more important for building culture than what employees see from their leaders. If leaders are regularly scheduling meetings during lunch, it’s a signal that the break isn’t protected. Latest employees in particular pick up such signals, and quickly learn which behaviors are associated with success (and failure) in their new team or organization. Your own calendar also sends a powerful message. Protecting and taking your lunch break is critical, as is extending the same respect to your team during their breaks. These small, visible behaviors speak louder than words. 3. Treat skipped lunches as an important signal Understanding and measuring workplace culture requires listening in different ways. Surveys alone don’t cut it. Paying attention to skipped lunches can be part of that strategy. And while working through lunch might ultimately be a personal preference, when it becomes the norm, it tells you something about your organization. If employees feel they can’t step away for even 30 minutes without falling behind, that’s a strong signal that the always-on mentality is rampant in your organization. Burnout in these cultures can be prolific, and workloads, staffing levels, and meeting demands should be questioned. But consider the unwritten expectations, too. What happens when employees say no? Is their commitment to the team or organization questioned? Are they no longer seen as top performers? 4. Use lunch to make human connection easier Lunch offers us much of what the front porch did: unstructured time together. No agendas, no project tasks, no scheduled meetings. Instead, employees have space and time to build connections and relationships within and beyond their immediate teams. That’s especially important for younger workers. Gen Z employees have 47% increased odds of saying they can’t find community at work, and 32% increased odds of saying technology makes it difficult to disconnect from work. This research demonstrates that while technology makes it easier to stay in contact, it doesn’t guarantee genuine relationships. Employees can be constantly reachable and still feel they don’t know their colleagues at all. Lunchtime gives employees room for conversations that aren’t tied to a project, deadline, or key performance indicator. When we protect this space, we create organic opportunities to build relationships and communities that are much more difficult to develop through structured interaction. 5. Reward outcomes instead of constant availability Employees pay attention to who and what is getting recognized. If you want to shift behavior, change what you reward. Recognition is a powerful tool for change management. Focus recognition on the outcomes and behaviors you want to encourage. Make it clear that high performance doesn’t require employees to prove they’re always available. When organizations reinforce behaviors through integrated recognition, they see a 43% reduction in early warning signs of burnout. The focus on outcomes becomes even more important as AI increases the speed and capacity of work. When employees can accomplish more in less time, resist the temptation to fill every available minute with more work. Be deliberate about rewarding strong outcomes rather than constant activity. The case for keeping lunch on the calendar As technology makes it easier to stay connected and accomplish more throughout the day, protecting time for a real break gets harder. Push back on that pressure by establishing clear boundaries and modeling them yourself. Giving employees permission to pause creates room to recover and connect, while reinforcing that performance doesn’t depend on always-on expectations. How you approach lunch reflects the broader expectations you set for your workplace. By making breaks a regular part of the day, you can help establish healthier habits that become a lasting part of your culture.

The point is to create a culture where stepping away feels like a normal choice. And it requires looking at the signals your workplace sends about availability, performance, and connection.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Create space that can’t automatically become another meeting.

If every open block on a calendar is considered schedulable, lunch will always be at risk. Consider establishing meeting-free windows during the day so employees have protected time to recharge.

Sources indicate that adapt that approach for global and frontline teams instead of assuming the same time works for everyone. Employees across time zones and operating environments may need different windows, but the principle is the same: Build recovery into the work day.

In a recent development, 2. Model the behavior you want.

Culture is a collection of the norms, values, and behaviors that employees see around them every day. And nothing is more important for building culture than what employees see from their leaders. If leaders are regularly scheduling meetings during lunch, it’s a signal that the break isn’t protected. Upcoming employees in particular pick up such signals, and swiftly learn which behaviors are associated with success (and failure) in their new team or organization.

Sources indicate that your own calendar also sends a powerful message. Protecting and taking your lunch break is critical, as is extending the same respect to your team during their breaks. These small, visible behaviors speak louder than words.

3. Treat skipped lunches as an important signal.

Sources indicate that understanding and measuring workplace culture requires listening in different ways. Surveys alone don’t cut it. Paying attention to skipped lunches can be part of that strategy. And while working through lunch might ultimately be a personal preference, when it becomes the norm, it tells you something about your organization.

If employees feel they can’t step away for even 30 minutes without falling behind, that’s a strong signal that the always-on mentality is rampant in your organization. Burnout in these cultures can be prolific, and workloads, staffing levels, and meeting demands should be questioned.

It has been revealed that but consider the unwritten expectations, too. What happens when employees say no? Is their commitment to the team or organization questioned? Are they no longer seen as top performers?

According to recent reports, 4. Use lunch to make human connection easier.

Lunch offers us much of what the front porch did: unstructured time together. No agendas, no project tasks, no scheduled meetings. Instead, employees have space and time to build connections and relationships within and beyond their immediate teams.

In a recent development, that’s especially important for younger workers. Gen Z employees have 47% increased odds of saying they can’t find community at work, and 32% increased odds of saying technology makes it difficult to disconnect from work.

According to recent reports, this research demonstrates that while technology makes it easier to stay in contact, it doesn’t guarantee genuine relationships. Employees can be constantly reachable and still feel they don’t know their colleagues at all.

Lunchtime gives employees room for conversations that aren’t tied to a project, deadline, or key performance indicator. When we protect this space, we create organic opportunities to build relationships and communities that are much more difficult to develop through structured interaction.

5. Reward outcomes instead of constant availability.

Recent findings suggest that employees pay attention to who and what is getting recognized. If you want to shift behavior, change what you reward. Recognition is a powerful tool for change management.

Sources indicate that focus recognition on the outcomes and behaviors you want to encourage. Make it clear that high performance doesn’t require employees to prove they’re always available. When organizations reinforce behaviors through integrated recognition, they see a 43% reduction in early warning signs of burnout.

According to recent reports, the focus on outcomes becomes even more key as AI increases the speed and capacity of work. When employees can accomplish more in less time, resist the temptation to fill every available minute with more work. Be deliberate about rewarding strong outcomes rather than constant activity.

As technology makes it easier to stay connected and accomplish more throughout the day, protecting time for a real break gets harder.

Industry observers note that push back on that pressure by establishing clear boundaries and modeling them yourself. Giving employees permission to pause creates room to recover and connect, while reinforcing that performance doesn’t depend on always-on expectations.

How you approach lunch reflects the broader expectations you set for your workplace. By making breaks a regular part of the day, you can help establish healthier habits that become a lasting part of your culture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Police in Canada are searching for at least three suspects after thieves crashed a stolen SUV through the front of a video game store before escaping in a waiting getaway vehicle.

The incident occurred in the early hours of November 26, just one week after the release of GTA 6, at We Got Gamez in Whitby, Ontario, leaving the business temporarily closed as its owners assess the damage.

According to Durham Regional Police, officers responded to reports of a break-in at approximately 2:55 AM.

Recent findings suggest that two suspects exited a black SUV after driving it through the storefront before fleeing in a second vehicle. Police later confirmed that the SUV used in the break-in had been stolen.

The store was unoccupied at the time, and no injuries were reported. Authorities have not disclosed what merchandise was taken or its value.

In a series of Instagram posts, We Got Gamez shared its devastation over the incident but promised customers that the business would bounce back.

“Folks this is getting out of hand. Last night our Whitby Location was violated and broken into,” the store wrote.

A post shared by We Got Gamez (@wegotgamez1).

The owners estimate that the location will remain closed for 10 to 14 days as they clean up, account for missing merchandise, replace fixtures, and ensure the building is structurally safe for customers.

“Mike and I have had our emotional moments and now it’s game time. We promise you We Got Gamez Whitby will be back and better than ever,” the store added.

Police can’t wait for GTA 6 to be released so they can “catch a break”.

Armed burglars smash into GameStop and hit officer with car to escape cops.

Rockstar Games responds to massive GTA 6 gameplay leaks from CyberLeek.

The owners also thanked the local gaming community for visiting the damaged store and offering their support following the break-in.

“Means the world and is our secret power to get back up and running.”.

A post shared by We Got Gamez (@wegotgamez1).

We Got Gamez’s other locations in the GTA, Ajax and Mississauga will remain open while repairs are underway in Whitby, but the store is warning customers not to literally crash into those stores for their Black Friday door-crasher deals.

Meanwhile, police are asking anyone with information, surveillance footage, or dashcam recordings of the incident to come forward.

If you're not using Auto Drive and Cinematic Camera in GTA 6, you're missing out on some of the best experiences in the game

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have just successfully busted a Kingfisher operation just north of Cottonmouth Lake in Mariana County.
  • Sources indicate that "That one was for Donnie," Lucia indicates to Jason as they get in their favourite car - Jason's sunset yellow Declasse '72 Tulip, with a suped up engine and custom parts.
  • Recent findings suggest that so, hopping into the car, hitting 'down' on the D-Pad and then hitting 'Start' will instigate the Cinematic Camera, and if you've already set a destination on the map or via the handy upcoming quick navigational menu (simply hold 'down' to see this), your chosen lovebird will start automatically driving to their next location.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers for Chapter 1-3 of GTA 6 follow.

I have just successfully busted a Kingfisher operation just north of Cottonmouth Lake in Mariana County. It was beautiful. Jason took point, armed with a shotgun liberated from an M7 clubhouse, guarding a chokepoint as hordes of rednecks threw themselves at him in an unceremonious, slightly humiliating pantomime of existential futility. Lucia, confident in her improving gunmanship, stood behind, aimed over Jason's broad shoulders, and took out stragglers with a custom hunting rifle pilfered from the Kingfisher's own safehouse. Not so safe anymore, is it, losers? This one's for Donnie, I think as I kneecap the final goon and rifle through their safe.

Sources indicate that "That one was for Donnie," Lucia indicates to Jason as they get in their favourite car - Jason's sunset yellow Declasse '72 Tulip, with a suped up engine and custom parts. God damn, I think, this game can read my mind. And I'm not sure if I would have had this intimate little moment of grief and reconciliation if I hadn't got in the habit of using the game's Cinematic Camera. Your dual protagonists can chat even when you, the player, are in the driving seat - of course - but there's so much going on in the world of Leonida (and so many pedestrians and motorists that like to behave like maniacs and cut you off) that I find their conversations are often cut short or terminated altogether by the chaos of the world.

Recent findings suggest that so, hopping into the car, hitting 'down' on the D-Pad and then hitting 'Start' will instigate the Cinematic Camera, and if you've already set a destination on the map or via the handy upcoming quick navigational menu (simply hold 'down' to see this), your chosen lovebird will start automatically driving to their next location. For me, in this example, it was the Pelican River to Vice City's Bayside, and Boobie's apartment. Probably about 15 minutes of real-world time; enough space to fuss my dog, grab a drink, reply to my editor, and really take the time to soak in the absurd level of detail Rockstar has crammed into its opus. On this specific journey, I also heard a really touching, sweet interaction about Jason's insecurities regarding Lucai's mum. Goosebumps.

GTA 6 is an action-packed game; there aren't a lot of menial jobs going for Jason and Lucia - they're on the run, after all, so I don't think a traditional PAYE-compliant nine-to-five is really on the cards. As such, even the smaller money-making activities on offer are quite stressful: dirt-track events, street racing, pawn store robberies, hit-and-runs, stick-ups… there's only so much a bit of meditation in a park can do to decompress you. So I've taken to enjoying life on the roads. After a substantial, somewhat impromptu heist on two Kingfisher operations, I need a bit of time to slow down and smell the proverbial roses (or should that be Tulips?).

Jumping into Jason's car, turning the radio to The Chamber 106.6, and letting the star-crossed lovers meander their way home listening to Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya play a selection of metal tracks from the past four decades is good for my brain. I actually think these moments of leisure are essential to the rhythm of GTA 6: dial it up, cool it off. It creates this almost tidal ebb and flow, the resultant flotsam and jetsam ending up fenced or stashed as the rhythm dictates.

I'm usually a very active and fussy player when it comes to games; I can't stand long cutscenes taking control away from me, and I absolutely will skip story scenes on a second playthrough if it's getting in the way of hands-on controller time. So I'm quite surprised at the ease with which I've given up my agency for these longer rides. But it's a testament to Rockstar's writing. I want to see what Jason and Lucia are saying to each other. I want the camera to show me the world passing me by outside my window as I get from A to B. I even sometimes schedule and phase in little detours to C and D, to be honest, because I feel so zen as I watch the bruise-coloured sky sets over the Keys (and I want to hear the end of Symphony of Destruction, maybe).

Sources indicate that my Lucia is dressed a bit like someone you'll see cutting about outside Nottingham's Rock City club - cute little tank top, leather jacket, nose and ear piercings galore. One afternoon, after driving out to Hamlet to have a long overdue catch-up with her mum, I set the Cinematic Camera and auto-drive settings on to take her back to meet Jason at a bar (another place, incidentally, you can turn on the Cinematic Camera and just watch them hang out together). On her way back home, with the sunlight dipping below the horizon, the fiery orange ambience caught the whites of her eye and the metallic zip of her leather jacket. She smiled to herself as Tool's Sober came on the radio. Christ, I thought, I'm there.

GTA 6 has this odd capacity to transport me. I think it's because the levels of simulation in Leonida are so artisanal, so well-pitched, and so well-executed. I can believe I'm there. I want to sit in this muscle car, no doubt smelling of leather and oil, listening to Tool with Lucia. I want to feel the humid air of Watson Bay coalescing on my skin, warm air blowing through my hair. I want to join in on Jason and Lucia's in-jokes, laugh as they do little impressions of each other and coo as they make up and hold hands during the longer drives. I want to stick my head out the window like Lucia does and smell the Cuban food grilling in the food trucks, or hear the kids partying on the beach.

With the Cinematic Camera turned on, I have the chance to do that. I don't have to worry about making money, paying back favours I owe, checking in with Brian, topping up my BuckMe account. I can just engage in this fantasy - this simulation - Rockstar has built for me. And in these moments where I take my hands off the wheel, hang out with these people I've dressed up and ride around in the car I've built, it really does feel like it's been made just for me. I can't remember the last time a game made me feel that way.

  • In today’s fast-changing tech landscape, customer expectations are evolving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before I debuted my own manufacturer, I worked as a web developer for a New York media company. One of my colleagues was a coding savant. They could build a webpage in mere hours, an incredible feat in the early aughts. They could identify bugs and rapidly come up with smart solutions. But they also frequently disappeared in the middle of the workday and took personal days with little to no notice. My colleague was reliable in their work, but not dependable day-to-day. Employees—and organizations—need both to provide real value. In today’s fast-changing tech landscape, customer expectations are evolving. Customers expect businesses to be reliable and digital experiences to work as promised. At the same time, they’re becoming wary of the tech race. In a recent survey of about 3,500 U.S. consumers about their digital lives, 77% mentioned tech companies focus more on outpacing the competition than on solving real user problems. What separates leading organizations in the AI era is not reliability alone, but dependability at every step. Here’s how leaders and organizations can deliver on that promise. Make every customer experience consistent Having a product or service work the way you need it to is notable. No doubt, customers take note. In the above-mentioned survey, three-quarters of consumers reported that new tech features improved their lives and that digital experiences were becoming more personalized. At the same time, fewer than 30% said they strongly agree with that sentiment. The takeaway for businesses: There’s room for improvement. Where can businesses identify those areas for improvement? One strategy is ensuring that the entire user experience is 24/7 consistent. Every interaction along the customer journey, from initial inquiries to troubleshooting, should provide the same level of care and attention. Artificial intelligence can help make that possible. Customized AI agents, for example, can respond to common inquiries around the clock. When faced with more complex or nuanced issues, they can escalate the matter to human representatives. This ensures customers can connect with your company whenever they need to, and without requiring employees to be always on. Consistency also means ensuring customers receive the same information across channels, whether they’re perusing the website, DMing with a chatbot via an app, or speaking with an employee on the phone. For customers, the result isn’t just a reliable product or service—it’s feeling heard and seen. That’s where dependability makes a difference. Customers build trust when every interaction feels responsive and aligns with what the organization has promised. Ensure every interaction feels like your brand Every interaction between customers and your company is an opportunity to build a relationship—or weaken an existing one. Especially in the age of AI, your company’s voice has to be cohesive, whether customers are chatting with an employee or a chatbot. As noted in Harvard Business Review, chatbots are becoming the frontline of customer interactions—and they can shape how customers perceive your brand, from its personality and values to its approach to customer service. What’s more, the HBR article highlights research showing that people who interacted with a warm, supportive AI companion felt closer to the chatbot than to colleagues, acquaintances, and even friends. People of a more task-oriented assistant, on the other hand, felt less connected to it than to their human relationships. The implication for brands: How AI communicates impacts the customer experience, as well as the kind of relationship customers believe they have with a company. For starters, customer-facing AI tools should reflect your brand identity. With a chatbot, for example, you can begin by defining its personality; whether it’s a supportive coach, an empathetic companion, or a sophisticated advisor. Decide the kind of information it handles and when conversations should be handed off to a human. AI-powered chatbots should do more than just sound like your brand. They should deliver the kind of relationship that reflects your company’s mission and values. Anticipate customer needs and act on them In the AI era, one of the biggest competitive advantages is anticipating customers’ needs, sometimes even before they’re aware of them. Consider a large language model like ChatGPT, which predicts what you might need next, encouraging users to continue engaging with it. For instance, you prompt ChatGPT to generate an outline; it does, then asks whether you’d like a draft introduction as well. Whether or not you say yes is your choice, but the option is there. Today’s companies can leverage AI to anticipate needs, streamline service, and resolve issues faster. AI-powered platforms like Chorus.ai can analyze customer interactions, synthesize sentiments, and flag recurring pain points. Then, your employees can better understand the customer experience and focus on developing solutions. Looking forward, AI-powered tools like Thematic can identify emerging trends and themes, helping companies evolve their products and services to remain competitive. As the founder of a company that began with online forms and has continually expanded its offerings over the past two decades, I know firsthand the importance of adapting to changing needs and spotting market opportunities. Importantly, AI is not error proof. Humans should always be kept in the loop to review decisions that impact the customer experience. Be transparent about AI use and jump in if and when AI falls short. That kind of behavior builds dependability and, on the customer side, reinforces loyalty.

#230512. Julia Fox wants to pay women back for splitting bills on dates with men

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1276 w)

Julia Fox wants to pay women back for splitting bills on dates with men

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women are fed up with being asked to split the bill on first dates.
  • In a recent development, women are fed up with being asked to split the bill on first dates.
  • If you’ve been dating in recent years, you’re aware that it’s a dumpster fire of an ordeal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women are fed up with being asked to split the bill on first dates. And now, Julia Fox, the actress and activist, is coming to the rescue. If you’ve been dating in recent years, you’re aware that it’s a dumpster fire of an ordeal. Between conversations on dating apps that never go anywhere, unsolicited nudes, and a slew of unoriginal conversationalists, the only consistent thing about modern dating is low effort. When it comes to women who are actively dating, it’s one of their biggest complaints—especially when it comes time to pay the tab. While it was once a standard practice in heteronormative romantic connections for men to pay the bill on a first date, women have been getting vocal about the fact that chivalry seems to be very, very dead. And they are over it. The frustration comes as the cost of dating seems to be rising in lockstep with men’s perceived low effort. According to upcoming research from the dating platform Seeking, 61% of Gen Z women have been asked to split the bill on a first date. That’s more than twice the rate of boomer women (27%) who have been asked to do the same. Meanwhile, 75% of women say they appreciate it when a man pays (like . . . duh?). The gap could explain, in part, why so many women say they’ve given up on dating. According to a Pew Research Center study published in 2023, fewer than 35% of single women say they’re seeking romantic relationships, compared with 54% of single men. Enter the Anti 50/50 Campaign, a movement led by Fox that aims to address one of women’s biggest gripes with modern dating. The campaign allows women who’ve been asked to go halfsies on a date to apply for reimbursement. All they have to do is create a profile on Seeking’s website, share the details of the experience, and upload a receipt of the date’s bill. Those who are selected will be reimbursed up to $50. The $50,000 reimbursement fund will be open until February 10, 2027, or until all the money has been claimed. “I think we need to get over the idea that women should have to justify what they want out of dating,” Fox said in a press release. “I’m all for women being independent, but that doesn’t mean we have to entertain low-effort men who think splitting a check is the height of romance. If you’re going to court somebody, COURT THEM.”  The campaign certainly aims to raise awareness about a common pink flag. But it also speaks to the fact that women don’t earn as much on the dollar as men. So many modern men seem to have forgotten that there’s still a glaring pay gap that hurts women’s financial stability. According to a recent report from the Center for American Progress, the pay gap has barely budged since the year 2000. In 2025, women workers made $13,760 less annually than men. Women who worked full-time earned around 84 cents for every dollar made by male counterparts. “We’re giving women their money back while encouraging men to lead with generosity,” notes Dana Rosewall, CEO of Seeking. “Somewhere along the way, the patriarchy convinced women that splitting the bill was empowerment, when really it just made being cheap socially acceptable.”  In other words, if men are wondering whether or not women notice or appreciate it when they offer to pay for a first date, the short answer is: Yes, they do. It’s not just about money. It’s about effort, and not glossing over what may be easy for men to miss, but women surely don’t: that financial equality hasn’t quite arrived, no matter how hard women have worked to tip the scale.

#230510. How to navigate the holiday party season while sober

How to navigate the holiday party season while sober

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2426 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when Tat Read decided to give up alcohol four years ago to support a family member who was struggling with addiction, she knew that her career would present some obstacles.
  • When Tat Read decided to give up alcohol four years ago to support a family member who was struggling with addiction, she knew that her career would present some obstacles.
  • In a recent development, “Being in the industry that I’m in, I’m always at parties; I’m always at dinners,” indicates the 45-year-old communications professional.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when Tat Read decided to give up alcohol four years ago to support a family member who was struggling with addiction, she knew that her career would present some obstacles. “Being in the industry that I’m in, I’m always at parties; I’m always at dinners,” claims the 45-year-old communications professional. “My job is about bringing people together. And when people are brought together, there’s always alcohol on the table.” Read, who says she was never much of a drinker to begin with, started limiting her consumption to a drink or two at work-related events about five years ago. As a mother of four, however, she found that even a small amount was more trouble than it was worth. “My kids are really young. I have to be up early in the morning, and it was starting to affect my sleep,” she says. “It just had downstream impacts that I really wasn’t appreciating.” Read says her colleagues supported her decision to give up alcohol completely, but says it’s still hard to navigate professional situations with fresh people, like networking events. “I had trepidation about being fully sober because I knew it was an awkward conversation to have,” she says. “Sometimes I will hold a glass of sparkling water instead of champagne to not feel like I need to explain myself.” Read isn’t the only one who occasionally finds strategies to avoid conversations about her sobriety. According to a recent survey by the Boca Recovery Center, which operates addiction treatment centers in Florida, Indiana, Massachusetts, and New Jersey, 39% of Americans who abstain from alcohol hide their sobriety at work and 30% fake it to blend in—like drinking sparkling water from a champagne flute. And 13% have skipped a work event, celebration, or date to avoid the topic altogether. Given that more than half of sober Americans have been questioned, pressured, or teased about their decision not to consume alcohol, according to the survey, it is perhaps no surprise that 58% hide it from at least some people in their lives, and that 13% haven’t told anyone. “The holidays make this harder, as events tend to be based around drinking,” says Alison Tarlow, a licensed clinical psychologist who is the chief clinical officer at Boca Recovery Center. “Those hiding their sobriety are managing a drink, an excuse and a conversation all at once—which is socially exhausting in a setting that is supposed to be fun and relaxed.” Stigma remains even as more Americans go sober More Americans are choosing to go alcohol-free for a wide variety of reasons, though taboos related to addiction and mental health remain. According to the survey, one in four Americans have experimented with alcohol-free or reduced-drinking challenges; half of these cite physical or mental health-related reasons, compared with 10% who were recovering from addiction. Against this backdrop, younger generations appear less likely than others to hide their sobriety. According to the survey, only 5% of Gen Z keep it a secret, compared with 12% of millennials and 20% of Gen Xers. But these younger Americans also face the most outside stigma, as 68% of sober Gen Zs have faced questioning, pressure, or teasing compared with 49% of older sober Americans. “Telling people tends to involve fielding questions, which is generally off-putting to those who made such a personal decision,” says Tarlow. “Sobriety is a complex and sensitive decision, and people want to choose who hears about it and when.” Navigating the holiday party season without alcohol The holidays can be an especially challenging time for those who are looking to stay sober. Between personal and professional events, family and financial obligations ramping up, and work responsibilities starting to dwindle, many are left without some of the support systems, practical reasons, or reminders that help them maintain sobriety. Though they may feel judged for ordering an alcohol-free alternative, 93% of Americans say they would not think less of a coworker who skips alcohol at a work event, according to the survey. “The judgment sober people anticipate is usually harsher than what their peers tend to think,” says Tarlow. While colleagues may ask questions, she emphasizes that those who choose sobriety don’t need to explain themselves. “’I’m not drinking tonight’ is perfectly fine,” Tarlow says. “These events are meant to be fun, so focus on enjoying yourself, not others’ expectations. But, if pressure builds, there’s no shame in taking a break or leaving.” Coming up with excuses for not drinking can be exhausting and dishonest, says Phillip Barbb, an executive coach who specializes in sobriety. “You don’t want to feel like you have to have 25 conversations where you’re lying at the holiday party,” he says. “Creating this false narrative for yourself can weigh on you, because you’re building a gap between yourself and others.” Instead, Barbb, who has been sober for almost 19 years himself, suggests preparing a short explanation in advance that feels authentic and genuine, like, “I’m doing it for health reasons,” or “I decided I wanted to try not drinking this holiday season.” Some may also find it helpful to create a practical reason for staying sober to help them through workplace holiday events, like being a designated driver or making an early-morning commitment for the following day. Those trying to stick to their sobriety goals can also enlist the support of a colleague, date, or friend, though Barbb warns that these people shouldn’t be made responsible for someone else’s choices. “It is no one else’s responsibility to keep me sober or to keep me out of bad situations,” he says. “What I do think is cool is saying, ‘I want to go to the event, I don’t want to drink, so I may have a moment or two where I need to pull you aside to just talk or vent.’” How employers can offer more inclusive holiday parties for sober staff With so many Americans experimenting with sobriety—and so many hiding it from their colleagues—organizations will inevitably plan holiday parties for attendees who are abstaining from alcohol, whether the organization knows it or not. So it’s vital for employers to consider ways they can make the environment more inclusive for workers who don’t want to drink. When a holiday party’s primary activity is consumption, it can make those who are going sober stand out. That is why employers are encouraged to include other activities, like bowling, an escape room, or mini golf. Choice of venue can also play a role, as an event held at a bar or club may create more anxiety—and discourage more from attending—than one held at an activity venue or restaurant. “If you’re hosting an event, you do have a responsibility to offer more than just beer and wine so that people can feel comfortable,” Barbb adds. “If you’re offering signature drinks, do a version without alcohol.” Workplace cultures are often set at the top, meaning it’s up to leaders to model responsible behavior and signal inclusivity for sober attendees. “It’s not anybody’s job—nor is it their right—to pry into the lives of their employees. But you should still make sure that you’re creating environments that are safe for people to be in,” Barbb says. “For executives and leaders, your responsibility for your people continues even outside of work hours.”.

Converting Markdown to PDF is easy until the document has real content: long code blocks, wide tables, images and non-Latin text are where most tools fall apart.

Pandoc with LaTeX is still the most powerful route, but it needs a large install and trips over Unicode and emoji unless you switch engines and fonts.

Browser-based approaches (print CSS, Chromium-powered converters, in-browser tools) avoid the install and give you HTML-quality rendering, as long as you control page breaks.

A handful of print CSS rules (@page, break-inside: avoid, break-after: avoid) fix the majority of ugly PDFs, whichever tool you use.

Choose the tool by the document: a quick README export, a long technical report and a multilingual document each have a different best option.

I write almost everything in Markdown: READMEs, release notes, client handovers, meeting notes. And at least once a week, someone asks for "the PDF version". Every time, the conversion looks fine on the first page and falls apart somewhere around page three: a code block split in half, a table running off the edge, an emoji replaced by an empty box.

SitePoint covered the classic route back in 2015 with Creating PDFs from Markdown with Pandoc and LaTeX. That approach still works. But a lot has changed since then, and today there are several ways to get a clean PDF without installing a TeX distribution. This article compares them, then goes through the rendering problems you'll actually hit, with a fix for each.

Pandoc is still the Swiss Army knife. The simplest command is:.

Recent findings suggest that by default, that goes through LaTeX, which means you need a TeX distribution installed (several gigabytes for a full one). The output is beautiful for prose and math, but LaTeX has strong opinions about layout, and customizing it means writing LaTeX.

Pandoc can also render through an HTML engine instead, which lets you style the PDF with CSS:.

Best for: long documents, academic writing, math, automated pipelines.

Watch out for: install size, Unicode handling with the default engine (more on that below).

It has been revealed that render the Markdown to HTML (any previewer, a static site, a GitHub page) and print it to PDF. It's free and already installed everywhere, but you inherit whatever the page looks like on screen: navigation bars, sidebars, and page breaks wherever they happen to fall.

Best for: quick, one-off exports of short documents.

Watch out for: zero control over page breaks unless the page ships print CSS.

Extensions like Markdown PDF for VS Code, or CLI tools like md-to-pdf, render your Markdown to HTML and print it with a headless Chromium:.

In a recent development, you get the same rendering quality as a browser, plus a config file for CSS, margins, headers and footers. The trade-off is a Node install and a downloaded Chromium.

Best for: developers who live in their editor or want CI-friendly exports.

Watch out for: the first run downloads a browser, and print CSS is still your job.

Recent findings suggest that the newest option is tools that do the whole conversion inside the browser tab: you paste or drop the .md file, preview the actual pages and download the PDF. The good ones don't upload your file anywhere, which matters for client documents and internal notes.

Best for: people who don't want to install anything, non-developers on your team, private documents.

Watch out for: many online converters do upload your file to a server; check before you paste anything confidential.

Whichever method you pick, the same handful of problems show up as soon as the document is longer than a page. Most of them are fixed with print CSS, which works in Pandoc's HTML engines, Chromium-based tools and any HTML you print from a browser.

A 20-line function cut after line 3, with the rest on the next page, is the most common complaint. The fix is to ask the renderer not to break inside the block:.

One caveat: a block longer than a full page has to break. For those, it's better to let it break cleanly than to push it to a upcoming page and leave a huge gap.

According to recent reports, on screen, a long line in a code block scrolls horizontally. On paper, there's no scrollbar, so it's simply cut off. Wrap long lines in print:.

Tables with many columns overflow the page or get squeezed until every cell is one word per line. Three things help: a smaller font size for tables, a landscape page for the worst offenders, and avoiding breaks in the middle of short tables:.

If a table genuinely needs eight columns, consider whether it should be a table in the PDF at all, or an appendix in landscape.

A heading alone at the bottom of a page, with its content on the next one, looks broken. This rule keeps a heading attached to what follows it:.

Support for break-after: avoid varies between rendering engines, so test it with yours; when it isn't honored, a manual page break before the heading is the reliable fallback.

Markdown has no syntax for a page break. The usual trick is a raw HTML element that print CSS turns into a break:.

Some converters also recognize a comment like , which has the advantage of staying invisible when the same file is rendered on GitHub.

In a recent development, images are inserted at their natural size, so a 4000-pixel screenshot spills off the page. Cap them:.

For blurry images, the problem is usually the opposite: a small screenshot stretched to page width. Export screenshots at 2x if they're going into a PDF.

Industry observers note that this one is specific to the LaTeX route. With the default pdflatex engine, Unicode characters outside its supported set produce errors or simply vanish. Switch to XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX and give it a font that actually contains the characters:.

Emoji are harder still in LaTeX and often need a dedicated package. HTML-based renderers handle both far better, because they use the operating system's font fallback just like a web page does.

It has been revealed that internal links ([see setup](#setup)) and external links should stay clickable. HTML-based renderers usually keep both. If yours doesn't, check that headings get IDs (most Markdown parsers add them) and that the PDF engine preserves link annotations.

Put together, these rules make a solid starting point for any HTML-based route:.

Save it as print.css and pass it to Pandoc (--css=print.css with an HTML engine), to md-to-pdf through its config, or include it in the HTML you print from the browser.

My rule of thumb after a lot of trial and error:.

A quick README or notes export, no install, private content: an in-browser converter. Full disclosure: this need is why I built the free Markdown to PDF converter on AwesomeToolkit, and it's what I use for this case now. It renders real A4 or Letter pages as you type, has an option to keep code blocks and tables whole, adds page numbers and a table of contents, and the conversion happens in the browser, so the file isn't uploaded anywhere.

Documentation in a repo, exported in CI: md-to-pdf or Pandoc with an HTML engine, plus the stylesheet above.

Long reports, math, academic formatting: Pandoc with XeLaTeX, using a font that covers every script in the document.

Something you'll print once and forget: the browser's Print to PDF is fine.

According to recent reports, whatever you choose, the biggest quality jump comes from the print rules, not the tool. Ten lines of CSS turn "it looks fine until page three" into a PDF you can actually send.

Yes. Your browser's Print to PDF works on any rendered Markdown, and in-browser converters do the whole conversion in a tab. Check that the converter processes files locally if the content is private.

The default pdflatex engine has limited Unicode support. Use --pdf-engine=xelatex or lualatex and set a font that contains the characters with -V mainfont= (and -V CJKmainfont= for CJK text).

It has been revealed that markdown has no native syntax for it. Insert where you want the break, or use the page-break comment your converter supports.

Add pre { break-inside: avoid; } to your print CSS. Blocks longer than a page will still break, which is expected.

With HTML-based renderers, usually yes, both external links and links to headings inside the document. Test internal links in particular, since they depend on headings having IDs.

Clicks Communicator hits a supply chain snag, and it isn’t because of RAM

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.
  • Industry observers note that the Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be.
  • It has been revealed that last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery enhancement detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.

Industry observers note that the Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be. It was first introduced at CES earlier this year, with the main selling angle being the physically integrated keyboard. Clicks wants to target those who are looking for a second device, and the Communicator fits the bill.

It has been revealed that last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery enhancement detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes. However, Clicks posted a latest update today stating that the timeline has shifted out a month because of supply chain challenges caused by something other than RAM.

Unfortunately, we’ve encountered a delay with securing a critical supply chain component needed to fabricate our printed circuit board ahead of manufacturing and final assembly. Assembly will now begin in early January, with deliveries expected to start in late January.

It notes that the “critical supply chain component” is the essential fabric used for the company’s printed circuit boards. The blog post dives into some neat details about the component holding things up. The PCBs Clicks is using are made up of more material layers than some competitor boards. But the fabric used to layer those boards is in short supply at this sort of demand, with four manufacturers reportedly unable to meet the company’s required volume.

The post also spells out difficulties caused by troubles in the Middle East, and rising memory costs straining the chain of supply further, even if memory – surprisingly – isn’t the cause of this small delay. Those compounded complications have pushed production back, and owners are now told to expect their Clicks Communicator pre-orders to be shipped in late January, at the earliest. Many pre-orders will likely be shipped after that because of further time constraints before Chinese New Year.

In an act of good faith, Clicks says it’s including a set of 3.5mm wired headphones in each box for orders placed prior to today.

A push from December to January isn’t massive, and Clicks still seems to be making solid time on developing a form factor we don’t often see. You can still pre-order the Clicks Communicator starting at $649.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the greatest tech-related purchases I’ve made of late is a product with no technology in it.I was feeling overwhelmed by the assortment of laptops, tablets, and other gadgets accumulating around the house and finally decided to do something about it. That’s how I wound up with a 10-slot device organizer from a brand called MobileVision.I almost ordered the seven-slot version instead, but swiftly realized there’d be no trouble filling a few more spaces. I also snaked a USB-C cable up behind the organizer, so I can always be charging something.This simple accessory has been a revelation, and not just because it helped tidy up my office. In my head it also creates a default place to store everything, which means one thing less to think about. This must be what actually organized people feel like all the time, I guess.This story first appeared in Advisorator, Jared’s weekly tech advice newsletter. Sign up to get free tech tips every Tuesday.The device organizer isn’t the only way I’ve been trying to tidy up my gadget situation. Here are a handful of other solutions I’ve accumulated over the years:Retractable chargersI mentioned retractable charging cables back in my year-end list of favorite tech things. The Baseus charging station on my desk (seemingly discontinued, though I’m happy with it) has a built-in cable I can pull out when my phone needs a top-up, while a separate Anker charger in the living room has a pair of retractable cables for the kids’ iPads. Both have cut down on the number of cables constantly dangling about.Charge connector adapters (with lanyards)While I’d love it if all my devices charged via USB-C, I’ve got a few stragglers that depend on Apple’s Lightning connector or the aging Micro USB standard. Instead of keeping separate cables around for these devices, I’ve decluttered by using little charging adapters that snap onto any USB-C connector.The key is to find ones with built-in lanyards, so they can hang onto to a USB-C cable even when they’re not plugged in. I use these Lightning-to-USB-C adapters for the aforementioned kids’ iPads, and have finally gotten around to buying a similar set for Micro USB.Cable tiesI am forever hoarding the velcro ties that sometimes come with charging cables, so I can use them to bunch various charging and data cables together. Huge packs of them are also available for cheap. (Alternatively, you can install cable hiders to keep things extra clean, but I’m reluctant to head down that rabbit hole.)Docking stations and standsPerhaps you noticed the lack of an iPad Pro to go with the Magic Keyboard in my organizer. That’s because it has its own magnetic charging stand in front of my desk, where I often use the iPad to take interview notes.Beyond that, I bought this cheap 3-in-1 Anker charging stand years ago, and it remains a nightstand fixture both at home and on the road. It works with any phone and earbuds with wireless charging, and you can snake a third charging cable through the USB-A port underneath. (Ostensibly, it’s for Apple Watches, but I’ve used it for other things as well.) I’ve also got a Steam Deck docking station that keeps it fully charged.I’m not saying you need to go on a massive organizational spree right now, but over time these little improvements have brought some much-needed order to my device empire. Perhaps they’ll give you some ideas of your own.Alternatively, you might just be thinking that I have too many gadgets sitting around to begin with. I was feeling overwhelmed by the assortment of laptops, tablets, and other gadgets accumulating around the house and finally decided to do something about it. That’s how I wound up with a 10-slot device organizer from a brand called MobileVision.

Industry observers note that I almost ordered the seven-slot version instead, but swiftly realized there’d be no trouble filling a few more spaces. I also snaked a USB-C cable up behind the organizer, so I can always be charging something.

Recent findings suggest that this simple accessory has been a revelation, and not just because it helped tidy up my office. In my head it also creates a default place to store everything, which means one thing less to think about. This must be what actually organized people feel like all the time, I guess.

Industry observers note that this story first appeared in Advisorator, Jared’s weekly tech advice newsletter. Sign up to get free tech tips every Tuesday.

The device organizer isn’t the only way I’ve been trying to tidy up my gadget situation. Here are a handful of other solutions I’ve accumulated over the years:.

I mentioned retractable charging cables back in my year-end list of favorite tech things. The Baseus charging station on my desk (seemingly discontinued, though I’m happy with it) has a built-in cable I can pull out when my phone needs a top-up, while a separate Anker charger in the living room has a pair of retractable cables for the kids’ iPads. Both have cut down on the number of cables constantly dangling about.

While I’d love it if all my devices charged via USB-C, I’ve got a few stragglers that depend on Apple’s Lightning connector or the aging Micro USB standard. Instead of keeping separate cables around for these devices, I’ve decluttered by using little charging adapters that snap onto any USB-C connector.

Industry observers note that the key is to find ones with built-in lanyards, so they can hang onto to a USB-C cable even when they’re not plugged in. I use these Lightning-to-USB-C adapters for the aforementioned kids’ iPads, and have finally gotten around to buying a similar set for Micro USB.

In a recent development, I am forever hoarding the velcro ties that sometimes come with charging cables, so I can use them to bunch various charging and data cables together. Huge packs of them are also available for cheap. (Alternatively, you can install cable hiders to keep things extra clean, but I’m reluctant to head down that rabbit hole.).

In a recent development, perhaps you noticed the lack of an iPad Pro to go with the Magic Keyboard in my organizer. That’s because it has its own magnetic charging stand in front of my desk, where I often use the iPad to take interview notes.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, I bought this cheap 3-in-1 Anker charging stand years ago, and it remains a nightstand fixture both at home and on the road. It works with any phone and earbuds with wireless charging, and you can snake a third charging cable through the USB-A port underneath. (Ostensibly, it’s for Apple Watches, but I’ve used it for other things as well.) I’ve also got a Steam Deck docking station that keeps it fully charged.

I’m not saying you need to go on a massive organizational spree right now, but over time these little improvements have brought some much-needed order to my device empire. Perhaps they’ll give you some ideas of your own.

Alternatively, you might just be thinking that I have too many gadgets sitting around to begin with. But that is a problem for another day.

AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

Sources indicate that the results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Industry observers note that using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

In a recent development, importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

It has been revealed that another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.

In a recent development, the findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

Sources indicate that "Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

Recent findings suggest that sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

In a recent development, immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

It has been revealed that because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer stated. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

Doctors right now rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

Industry observers note that the approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

It has been revealed that "In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

In a recent development, "Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a massive part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

According to recent reports, obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

Sources indicate that "It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer mentioned. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a significant return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Industry observers note that obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal Fresh Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Sources indicate that rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to upcoming insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most crucial contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer mentioned, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".

Google retiring Nest app and Google Assistant on speakers, displays in 2027

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Nest app on Android, iOS, and the web will stop working on January 25, 2027.
  • Officially, Google wants to “focus all of [its] engineering, security, and feature investments on one unified, modern experience.” It reiterated benefits like:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, following the Android deprecation in September, Google Assistant is going away on speakers and smart displays next year. Additionally, Google Home is fully replacing the Nest app in January.

The Nest app on Android, iOS, and the web will stop working on January 25, 2027. The Google Home app, which requires a Google Account, will be needed to “continue controlling and receiving notifications from your Nest devices remotely.”.

Officially, Google wants to “focus all of [its] engineering, security, and feature investments on one unified, modern experience.” It reiterated benefits like:.

Industry observers note that with home.nest.com going away, you have to download any custom video clips since they will not transfer over to Google Home. A one-click “Download All” button is available.

In a recent development, terrible news. For all my first-gen Nest cameras (wired hello doorbell, wired outdoor cams, and multiple indoor cams), I vastly prefer the Nest app to the terrible Google Home app.

It has been revealed that otherwise, Nest app consumers do not need to do anything else, with devices automatically transferring over to the Google Home app. No Nest thermostats, cameras, doorbells, smoke alarms, or locks are losing support with this change.

Additionally, Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions will automatically switch to Google Home Premium “with no additional cost and no credit card re-entry required at this time.”.

The other change declared today is that Google Assistant on speakers and smart displays is going away on August 2, 2027. It will be replaced by the Gemini for Home voice assistant. Google notes that natural language support replaces “rigid, static and highly specific voice commands.” Additionally:.

You can upgrade to Gemini today, while Google is expanding international availability over the coming months. Google will share more updates closer to the deadline.
